- [Guillermo Mantilla-Soler, Density questions on arithmetic equivalence (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1)
- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Ideal norms isolate first-degree primes

**Remember:** An inert quadratic prime enters at its square.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a nonzero prime ideal 𝔭 above a rational prime p, its norm is the cardinality of its residue field. This equals pᶠ, where f is the residue field degree over the field with p elements (our own).

**Problem.** In a number field of degree n, at most n√x prime ideals of norm ≤ x have degree greater than one. Hence the count of degree-one prime ideals is asymptotic to x/log x.

**How the definition helps.** An inert prime in ℚ(i) has norm p², so counting by p would include it too soon (our own). Every ideal of residue degree above one and norm at most x lies over p ≤ √x (our own). Each such p has at most n primes above it, giving the bound (our own). Landau’s prime ideal theorem counts all primes, and this bound is negligible compared with x/log x (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Landau prime ideal theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau_prime_ideal_theorem). It says: “the prime ideal theorem is dominated by the ideals of norm a prime number.”

**Sources:**

- [Edmund Landau, Neuer Beweis des Primzahlsatzes und Beweis des Primidealsatzes (1903)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01444310)

### Principal primes have reciprocal class-number density

**Remember:** Principal means identity in the Hilbert class field.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a number field K, its Hilbert class field H is the largest abelian extension unramified everywhere. This means finite primes acquire no repeated factors and real embeddings stay real. A principal ideal has one generator.

**Problem.** Among prime ideals of K, the proportion that are principal tends to 1/h. Count primes by residue field size, and let h count ideal classes, which identify ideals differing by a field scalar.

**How the definition helps.** The Hilbert class field turns the one-generator test into a test for complete splitting. Class field theory identifies ideal classes with automorphisms of H over K. A prime splits completely precisely when its class is the identity. Our own density calculation applies Chebotarev’s theorem to this one element in a group of size h.

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert class field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_class_field). It says: “Its degree over K equals the class number of K”

**Sources:**

- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Quarter turns let prime angles equidistribute

**Remember:** Take angles modulo the rotations made by units.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Every prime ideal of the Gaussian integers ℤ\[i\] has a generator a. Its four generators differ by multiplication by a power of i. Define the angle of the ideal as the argument of a modulo π/2.

**Problem.** Order these prime ideals by norm, the size of their residue field. The fraction with angle in any fixed subinterval of \[0,π/2) tends to the interval length divided by π/2.

**How the definition helps.** The generators a and ia give angles differing by π/2, which coincide in the quotient (our own). Thus each integer n gives a well-defined ideal character exp(4in arg a). For n ≠ 0 the Hecke prime ideal theorem makes its average over primes tend to zero (our own). Weyl’s criterion gives the stated interval proportions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hecke character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_character). It says: “The only units are powers of i, so the factor of 4 in the exponent ensures that the character is well defined on ideals.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Real places preserve principal-prime density

**Remember:** The ordinary class field keeps real places real.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The ordinary Hilbert class field is the largest abelian extension unramified everywhere. Its Galois group is commutative, finite primes acquire no repeated factors, and real embeddings stay real. Dropping the condition on real embeddings gives the narrow class field.

**Problem.** For K = ℚ(√3), all prime ideals split completely in its ordinary Hilbert class field. In its narrow class field, the proportion tends to one half when primes are ordered by residue field size.

**How the definition helps.** The real embedding condition excludes K(i), where a principal prime can fail to split. The cited example gives class number one, so the ordinary Hilbert class field equals K. The narrow class field is K(i), which has degree two over K. Our own calculation applies Chebotarev’s theorem to its identity automorphism.

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert class field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_class_field). It says: “in the extension K(i)/K there is ramification at the archimedean places”

**Sources:**

- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Split primes identify normal fields

**Remember:** Complete splitting detects the normal closure.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A prime splits completely in a finite extension if it has as many distinct prime factors as the extension degree. Attach to each finite Galois extension its set of completely split primes.

**Problem.** Two finite Galois extensions of a number field K inside one algebraic closure are equal if their completely split prime sets differ only finitely.

**How the definition helps.** In a common Galois closure, complete splitting tests whether Frobenius belongs to the subgroup fixing each field (our own). These subgroups are normal, so Chebotarev detects any difference on infinitely many primes (our own). Without normality, ℚ(∛2) shares its split primes with its Galois closure outside ramification (our own). Complete splitting there requires Frobenius to fix all three roots (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem). It says: “is uniquely determined by the set of primes of K that split completely in it.”

**Sources:**

- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Split primes intersect under composita

**Remember:** Fixing both fields fixes every element they generate together.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a finite Galois number field K, let S(K) contain the rational primes that split into \[K:ℚ\] distinct prime ideals. Equivalently, these primes are unramified and their Frobenius is the identity. Frobenius acts on residues by raising them to the power p.

**Problem.** For two finite Galois number fields K and L, S(KL) = S(K) ∩ S(L). In particular this intersection has natural density 1/\[KL:ℚ\].

**How the definition helps.** An automorphism fixes the field KL generated by K and L exactly when it fixes both fields. Our own argument uses this test for Frobenius in place of factoring p in KL. Primes unramified in both fields remain unramified in KL, and Frobenius restricts to Frobenius in each field. Chebotarev’s theorem gives the density of the identity class.

**Paper or page:** [Density questions on arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1). It says: “S(K̃L̃) = S(K̃) ∩ S(L̃).”

**Sources:**

- [Guillermo Mantilla-Soler, Density questions on arithmetic equivalence (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1)
- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Adele rings extend by tensoring

**Remember:** An extension just tensors the adeles once more.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A rational adele consists of a real number and one p-adic number for each prime p, integral at all but finitely many primes. Define the adele ring of K by tensoring the rational adele ring with K over ℚ. The usual construction takes tuples from the completions of K with the same integrality condition.

**Problem.** For finite extensions L/K of number fields, the adele ring of L is L tensored over K with the adele ring of K.

**How the definition helps.** The tensor definition makes the extension formula follow from associativity (our own). The work lies in identifying this ring with the usual ring of tuples (our own). Tensoring at each rational prime gives the product of the completions above it (our own). The corresponding rings of integers agree at all but finitely many primes (our own).

**nLab:** [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles). It says: “and the ring of adeles over k is the tensor product 𝔸ₖ ≔ k ⊗𝒪 𝔸𝒪.”

**Wikipedia:** [Adele ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adele_ring). It says: “If L/K is a finite extension of number fields, then the adelic construction is compatible with extension of scalars.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Adeles turn two classical theorems of number theory into one compactness statement

**Remember:** Multiply all local absolute values, require one, then identify global multiples.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups), 11R29, 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a number field K, an idele has a nonzero component in every completion and a unit component at almost every finite place. Its norm is the product of its normalized local absolute values (our own). The norm-one idele class group takes ideles of norm one modulo the diagonal copy of K× (our own).

**Problem.** For a number field K, the quotient of the norm-one ideles by K× is compact. This one statement is equivalent to the finiteness of the ideal class group together with Dirichlet's unit theorem.

**How the definition helps.** Finite valuations map norm-one idele classes onto the ideal class group, while logarithms at infinity describe the unit directions in the kernel (our own). The class group is discrete, so compactness requires finitely many classes (our own). Up to compact factors, the kernel is the logarithmic hyperplane modulo the unit lattice (our own). Its compactness is the full-rank assertion of Dirichlet’s unit theorem (our own).

**nLab:** [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles), [group of ideles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+ideles), [ideal class group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ideal+class+group). It says: “the finiteness of the ideal class group and the Dirichlet unit theorem are equivalent to a certain quotient of the ideles being compact and discrete.”

**Sources:**

- [Tom Weston, The idelic approach to number theory, lecture notes (undated)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PK0lPR7yq-1s1aooX4ZLr_zY4s2Ej36z/view)

### Finite ideles recover ideal classes

**Remember:** Forget the local units and keep the prime exponents.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Complete a number field at each finite prime, allowing limits in the distance defined by that prime. A finite idele chooses a nonzero element in each completion, with prime exponent zero at all but finitely many primes. Components with exponent zero are local units.

**Problem.** Divide the finite ideles by the tuples of local units and the nonzero field elements embedded diagonally. The result is the ordinary ideal class group, which identifies fractional ideals differing by a scalar.

**How the definition helps.** The unit condition ensures that the prime exponents of an idele specify a finite product of prime powers (our own). Every fractional ideal occurs because it factors into prime powers and each local field has an element of exponent one (our own). The local units form the kernel, and diagonal elements map to principal ideals (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Adele ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adele_ring). It says: “so the ordinary ideal class group is recovered as a quotient of the idele class group.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Ideles with almost all unit coordinates have unique normalized representatives over ℚ

**Remember:** One rational factor cancels every finite valuation and fixes the real sign.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A rational idele has one nonzero real entry and one nonzero p-adic entry per prime p, with valuation zero almost everywhere. Two ideles represent the same class if they differ by multiplication by one nonzero rational in every coordinate (our own).

**Problem.** Each class contains exactly one idele whose p-adic entries are all units and whose real entry is positive.

**How the definition helps.** Only finitely many valuations need clearing (our own). Divide by the product of p raised to the corresponding valuation, choosing its sign to make the real entry positive (our own). The only positive rational with valuation zero everywhere is one, giving uniqueness (our own).

**nLab:** [group of ideles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+ideles). It says: “The idele class group may be expressed as ℚ× ∖ 𝔸ℚ× ≃ (0,∞) × ∏ₚ ℤₚ×.”

### The idele class group states Artin reciprocity as one theorem

**Remember:** Quotient all ideles by diagonal global scalars.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups), 11R37. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The idele class group of a global field K is the quotient of its idele group by the diagonal subgroup K×.

**Problem.** For a number field K, the Artin map is surjective and factors through the idele class group. It gives an isomorphism from the idele class group modulo the connected component of 1 onto Gal(Kᵃᵇ/K).

**How the definition helps.** One quotient supplies a common domain for reciprocity at every finite abelian extension (our own). Global Artin reciprocity identifies its quotient by the identity component with the full abelian Galois group for number fields.

**nLab:** [Artin reciprocity law](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Artin+reciprocity+law), [class field theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/class+field+theory), [group of ideles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+ideles). It says: “says that this map is surjective, that it factors through the idele class group”

### The idele topology is finer than the subspace topology from the adeles

**Remember:** Give the ideles the topology that makes x ↦ x⁻¹ continuous.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The ideles 𝕀 are the units of the adeles 𝔸, the ring that combines all completions of a global field. The ideles get the topology of the subset {(x, x⁻¹)} of 𝔸 × 𝔸, not the subspace topology from 𝔸. Equivalently, this is the restricted-product topology with respect to the unit groups 𝒪ᵥ× of the local rings of integers.

**Problem.** With this topology the ideles form a topological group, in which multiplication and inversion are continuous. With the subspace topology from the adeles, inversion is not continuous.

**How the definition helps.** Inversion swaps the coordinates of (x,x⁻¹), and multiplication acts continuously in each coordinate (our own). Choose distinct finite primes and at each step replace just that prime’s component of 1 by a uniformizer (our own). These ideles converge to 1 in the adelic subspace topology (our own). Their inverses never enter the neighborhood requiring integrality at every finite place (our own).

**nLab:** [group of ideles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+ideles), [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles). It says: “Note: multiplicative inversion is not continuous in the subspace topology.”

**Sources:**

- [Tom Weston, The idelic approach to number theory, lecture notes](https://web.archive.org/web/20221205214531/https://people.math.umass.edu/~weston/oldpapers/idele.pdf)
- [Pete L. Clark, Adeles and Ideles, lecture notes](https://web.archive.org/web/20240508060418/http://alpha.math.uga.edu/~pete/8410Chapter6.pdf)

### The restricted product topology makes the adele ring locally compact

**Remember:** Keep compact integer rings in all but finitely many coordinates.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An adele of a global field K belongs to the product Uₛ of Kᵥ at places in S and Oᵥ elsewhere, for some finite S. Here S contains all archimedean places and Oᵥ denotes the local integer ring (our own). The restricted product topology makes every Uₛ open with its product topology.

**Problem.** The adele ring of a global field is locally compact. A global field is a number field or a function field of a curve over a finite field.

**How the definition helps.** Every adele belongs to an open Uₛ. The finitely many local fields there are locally compact, and the product of local integer rings outside S is compact by Tychonoff’s theorem (our own). Each Uₛ is therefore locally compact.

**nLab:** [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles). It says: “The restricted product is a filtered colimit of a system of open inclusions between locally compact Hausdorff rings, and is therefore itself locally compact Hausdorff.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The restricted product topology makes the rationals discrete in their adeles

**Remember:** Integral at every prime and smaller than one forces zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A rational adele has a real entry and one p-adic entry per prime p, integral at almost every prime. Basic open sets are products of local open sets whose p-adic factors equal ℤₚ at all but finitely many primes (our own).

**Problem.** The rational numbers, placed diagonally in the adeles of ℚ, form a discrete subgroup.

**How the definition helps.** With the restricted product topology, one open set around 0 constrains every prime at once (our own). A rational in every ℤₚ has no prime in its denominator, so it is an integer (our own). An integer with absolute value less than 1 is 0 (our own). The work moves to setting up the restricted product topology.

**Wikipedia:** [Adele ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adele_ring). It says: “The field K embeds diagonally in 𝔸ₖ as a discrete subring”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Trace pairings make adeles self-dual

**Remember:** The trace pairing glues the local character groups together.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a number field K, fix the standard additive characters ψᵤ of the completions of ℚ. For adeles x,y define their pairing as the product of ψᵤ(Trₖᵥ/ℚᵤ(xᵥyᵥ)) over all places v of K, with u below v (our own).

**Problem.** This pairing identifies the additive adele group of a number field with its continuous character group.

**How the definition helps.** Integral traces make almost every local character factor one, so each adele defines a global character (our own). Local trace duality gives a unique multiplier at each place for any continuous global character (our own). Continuity forces triviality on local integers almost everywhere, where the trace dual equals the integer ring (our own). Restricted product duality combines these multipliers into the required topological isomorphism (our own).

**nLab:** [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles). It says: “The additive group 𝔸ₖ is Pontrjagin self-dual in the sense that the map ϕ: 𝔸ₖ → 𝔸ₖ∧ induced from the pairing ⟨−, −⟩ is an isomorphism onto the character group.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Invertible ideals give the Picard group of an order

**Remember:** At a nonmaximal order, keep only ideals with inverses.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R65 (Class groups and Picard groups of orders). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an order R in a number field K, a fractional ideal is a nonzero finitely generated R-submodule of K. Such an ideal I is invertible if IJ = R for some fractional ideal J. The Picard group divides the group of invertible fractional ideals by the nonzero principal fractional ideals.

**Problem.** The Picard group of an order is isomorphic to the group of isomorphism classes of finitely generated modules locally free of rank one. Tensor product gives the group law.

**How the definition helps.** Restricting to invertible ideals makes cancellation valid even when the order lacks unique ideal factorization (our own). In ℤ\[2i\], the ideal I = 2ℤ\[i\] satisfies I² = 2I (our own). Cancellation would give I = 2ℤ\[2i\], although 2i belongs only to I (our own). The module description uses the theorem identifying invertibility with having a local basis of one element (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_domain). It says: “For an arbitrary domain one may define the Picard group Pic(R) as the group of invertible fractional ideals Inv(R) modulo the subgroup of principal fractional ideals.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Rationalization removes closed-point contributions

**Remember:** Finite residue K-groups disappear when you tensor with the rationals.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R70 (\\(K\\)-theory of global fields), 19D50. arXiv math.KT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the rational K-group of a ring in degree n by tensoring its integral K-group with ℚ. This kills every element of finite order.

**Problem.** Let A be the ring of integers of a number field and S any set of rational primes. Inverting S preserves all rational K-groups in degrees n ≥ 2.

**How the definition helps.** Quillen’s localization sequence places residue-field K-groups on either side of the localization map (our own). In degrees n and n−1 these groups are finite for n ≥ 2 by Quillen’s finite-field computation, so rationalization kills them (our own). Filtered colimits give the result for infinite S (our own). Integrally, {−1,3} in K₂(ℤ\[1/3\]) has nontrivial boundary modulo 3, excluding an integral lift (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory). It says: “then there is a long exact sequence”

- [Daniel Quillen, Higher algebraic K-theory I (1973)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0067053)

### Defining ramification index as a group index makes ramification indices multiply

**Remember:** Indices of nested groups multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 13F30. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let B dominate the discrete valuation ring A, meaning its maximal ideal contracts to that of A. Normalize the valuation v of B to have value group ℤ. Define e(B/A) as the index in ℤ of v(Frac(A)×) (our own).

**Problem.** For discrete valuation rings A ⊂ B ⊂ C with each inclusion local, e(C/A) = e(C/B)e(B/A).

**How the definition helps.** With the group-index definition, the theorem is the tower law for indices of subgroups (our own). The values taken on A, B and C form a chain of subgroups of ℤ under the valuation of C (our own). The work moves to proving that the index definition agrees with the ideal definition (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 15.112.3.](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BRL). It says: “Then the ramification indices of B/A and C/B multiply to give the ramification index of C/A.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining unramified as finite étale makes composita of unramified extensions unramified

**Remember:** Tensor the integer rings, then select the factor for the compositum.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 13B40. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A be a discrete valuation ring with fraction field K. Call a finite separable extension L/K unramified if the integral closure of A in L is finite étale over A (our own).

**Problem.** If L₁ and L₂ are finite separable unramified extensions of K inside one algebraic closure, then their compositum is unramified. The compositum is the smallest field that contains both.

**How the definition helps.** Tensoring the integral closures gives a finite étale A-algebra (our own). Since A is normal, this algebra is a product of normal domains (our own). Multiplication maps the generic tensor product onto the compositum, selecting a field factor (our own). Its integral closure is the corresponding finite étale domain factor, which proves unramifiedness (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 15.112.8.](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EXR). It says: “there exists a a finite separable extension L/K which is unramified with respect to A containing L₁ and L₂.”

### In upper numbering, abelian ramification jumps are integers

**Remember:** Weight lower time by the fraction of inertia still present.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite local Galois extension, let Gₓ be the lower group at ⌈x⌉. Set φ(s) = ∫₀ˢ \|Gₓ\|/\|G₀\| dx for s ≥ 0 and φ(s) = s on \[−1,0\] (our own). The upper group at φ(s) is Gₛ and jumps there if every sufficiently small positive increase changes the group (our own).

**Problem.** For a finite abelian extension of local fields, every jump of the upper ramification filtration is an integer.

**How the definition helps.** Upper numbering expresses abelian ramification in the integer steps of the local unit filtration (our own). Local reciprocity matches the positive upper groups with the images of those unit groups (our own). The integrality assertion is the Hasse–Arf theorem.

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse–Arf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%E2%80%93Arf_theorem), [Ramification group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramification_group), [Conductor (class field theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_%28class_field_theory%29). It says: “With the above set up of an abelian extension L/K, the theorem states that the jumps of the filtration {Gᵗ(L/K) : t ≥ −1} are all rational integers.”

### Reduced poles give ramification breaks

**Remember:** Remove p-divisible poles before reading the ramification break.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write a cyclic extension of degree p of K = k((t)), with k a finite field of characteristic p, as yᵖ − y = a. Replacing y by y + b changes a by bᵖ − b. Call a reduced when every negative power of t in a has exponent prime to p.

**Problem.** Suppose the reduced parameter a has a pole of order m. Then m is the unique positive ramification break in both lower and upper numbering.

**How the definition helps.** Reduction makes the pole order m prime to p, so v(t) = p and v(y) = −m yield a uniformizer tᵘyᵛ (our own). Choose integers u,v with pu−mv = 1, hence p does not divide v (our own). Each nonidentity automorphism translates y by a nonzero prime-field constant, changing this uniformizer by an element of valuation m+1 (our own). Thus the sole lower break is m, and upper numbering agrees through that break (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Artin–Schreier theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Schreier_theory). It says: “is the splitting field of an Artin–Schreier polynomial”

**Paper or page:** [Newton Polygons of Sums on Curves II: Variation in p-adic Families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08657v1). It says: “p<sup>j-1</sup>\\max \\{  k p<sup>-v<sub>p</sub>(c<sub>k</sub>)</sup>: v<sub>p</sub>(c<sub>k</sub>) &lt; j \\}  &amp;  \\text{if } v<sub>p</sub>(c<sub>k</sub>) &lt; j \\text{ for some } k”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Swan conductors ignore tame twists

**Remember:** Tame characters act trivially on every group the Swan conductor sees.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite local Galois group acting on a complex vector space V, the Swan conductor sums contributions from lower ramification groups Gᵢ for i ≥ 1. Each contributes \|Gᵢ\|/\|G₀\| times the codimension of its fixed space in V (our own). A tame character is a one-dimensional character trivial on G₁ (our own).

**Problem.** Twisting a complex representation of a finite local Galois group by a tame character leaves its Swan conductor unchanged.

**How the definition helps.** The sum leaves out the inertia group G₀, so it sees only groups on which a tame character is trivial (our own). Twisting multiplies each matrix by the character value, which is 1 on these groups, so every fixed space in the sum stays the same (our own). The Artin conductor also counts the G₀ term, which can change, even for a twist of the trivial representation (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Artin conductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_conductor). It says: “f(χ) − (χ(1) − χ(G₀))”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Tame ramification is exactly what a projective ring of integers needs

**Remember:** At every prime, the residue characteristic must be coprime to the ramification index.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11R33. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L/ℚ be finite Galois. For each prime p, let eₚ be the common exponent of the prime ideals in pOₗ. Call L tame if p does not divide eₚ for every p (our own).

**Problem.** For a finite Galois extension L of ℚ with group G, the ring of integers is a projective ℤ\[G\]-module exactly when L is tamely ramified. A projective module is a direct summand of a free module.

**How the definition helps.** Tameness gives one condition at each prime for the local normal integral basis theorem (our own). Noether’s theorem identifies these local conditions with projectivity of Oₗ over ℤ\[G\].

**Wikipedia:** [Galois representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_representation). It says: “Then Noether's theorem states that tame ramification is necessary and sufficient for OL to be a projective module over Z\[G\].”

**Sources:**

- [Emmy Noether, Normalbasis bei Körpern ohne höhere Verzweigung, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 167 (1932)](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1932.167.147)

### Tame ramification makes trace surjective

**Remember:** The trace of one is a unit across a tame totally ramified extension.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite extension of p-adic fields, tame means the ramification index is prime to the residue characteristic p. The ramification index is the valuation of a generator of the base maximal ideal, measured in the extension.

**Problem.** The trace on the rings of integers of a finite extension of p-adic fields is onto exactly when the extension is tame.

**How the definition helps.** In the totally ramified stage of degree e, trace sends one to e, a unit in the tame case (our own). The unramified stage has surjective trace by reduction to the finite residue fields (our own). In the wild case the totally ramified trace reduces to multiplication by e, hence vanishes on residues (our own). For example, ℚ₂(√2) has integral traces in 2ℤ₂ (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Ramification (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramification_%28mathematics%29). It says: “A finite generically étale extension B/A of Dedekind domains is tame if and only if the trace Tr: B → A is surjective.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Tameness gives the different exponent

**Remember:** Tame means the residue characteristic does not divide the ramification index.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite separable extension of non-Archimedean local fields with ramification index e is tame when the residue characteristic does not divide e. The different is the inverse of the trace dual of the ring of integers.

**Problem.** For a tame finite Galois extension of non-Archimedean local fields, the different has exponent e − 1.

**How the definition helps.** Tameness makes every higher ramification group trivial, so Hilbert’s formula ∑ (\|Gᵢ\| − 1) keeps only the inertia term e − 1 (our own). In the wild extension ℚ₂(√2), the derivative 2√2 of X² − 2 generates the different (our own). Its valuation is three, although e − 1 is one (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “is equal to e − 1 if P is tamely ramified”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Trace duality makes differents multiply

**Remember:** Trace in stages to multiply the different ideals.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite separable extension L/K of local fields, define the inverse different as the trace dual of the integers. It consists of x in L whose trace after multiplication by any integer of L is integral in K. The different is the inverse fractional ideal.

**Problem.** Let M/L/K be a tower of finite separable extensions of non-Archimedean local fields. The M/K different equals the M/L different times the extension of the L/K different to M.

**How the definition helps.** Transitivity tests the top trace in two stages (our own). For every y ∈ Oₘ one may also test all its multiples by Oₗ, so Trₘ/ₗ(xy) must belong to the L/K trace dual (our own). Dividing x by a generator of that dual leaves precisely the M/L trace-dual condition (our own). Inverting the resulting product gives the different formula (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “In a tower of fields L/K/F the relative differents are related by δ₍L/F₎ = δ₍L/K₎ δ₍K/F₎.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Trace duals make differents multiply

**Remember:** Trace duals compose because traces compose.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite separable extension of local fields, an integer is a field element of nonnegative valuation. The inverse different contains exactly those x for which the trace of xy is a base-field integer for every extension-field integer y. The different is its inverse as a fractional ideal, an ideal allowing denominators.

**Problem.** Consider a tower L/K/F of finite separable extensions of non-Archimedean local fields. The different of L/F equals the product of the different of L/K and the extended different of K/F.

**How the definition helps.** Trace transitivity makes products of the two trace-dual bases dual to the product integral basis (our own). These products therefore span the top inverse different and generate the product of the two inverse differents upstairs (our own). Inverting that identity gives the formula (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “In a tower of fields L/K/F the relative differents are related by δ(L/F) = δ(L/K)δ(K/F).”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Upper numbering makes ramification groups pass to quotients

**Remember:** Integrate the surviving fraction of inertia to convert lower time into upper time.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois extension of local fields, let Gₓ denote the lower group at index ⌈x⌉ for x ≥ −1 (our own). Set φ(u) = ∫₀ᵘ \|Gₓ\|/\|G₀\| dx for u ≥ 0 and φ(u) = u on \[−1,0\] (our own). Define Gᵗ as the lower group at φ⁻¹(t).

**Problem.** For a normal subgroup H of G, the image of Gᵗ in G/H is (G/H)ᵗ. This is Herbrand's theorem in upper numbering.

**How the definition helps.** Herbrand’s theorem identifies the lower quotient group after rescaling the index by the subgroup’s Herbrand function (our own). Composition of Herbrand functions then gives the same upper index for the image and the quotient group (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Ramification group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramification_group). It says: “The upper numbering is defined so as to be compatible with passage to quotients:”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 67, Springer (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Upper ramification indices rescale for subgroups

**Remember:** Restrict upper groups by changing their indices, not their elements.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Herbrand’s function φ turns lower ramification indices into upper ones. It is φ(u) = u for −1 ≤ u ≤ 0, and φ(u) = ∫₀ᵘ dt/\[G₀ : G<sub>t</sub>\] for u ≥ 0. The upper group at v is the lower group at ψ(v), where ψ is the inverse of φ.

**Problem.** Let M/K be a finite Galois extension of local fields and L/K a Galois subextension. Write ψ for the inverse change of index for L/K. For u ≥ −1, intersecting the upper group at u with Gal(M/L) gives the upper group for M/L at ψ(u).

**How the definition helps.** Lower indices pass to subgroups unchanged, so the rule follows by turning lower indices into upper ones in M/K and in M/L (our own). This translation uses ψ₍M/K₎ = ψ₍M/L₎ ∘ ψ₍L/K₎, which rests on Herbrand’s quotient theorem (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Ramification groups of some finite Galois extensions of maximal nilpotency class over local fields of positive characteristic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07928v4). It says: “Then we have $G<sup>i\\cap</sup> H=H<sup>\\psi (i)</sup>$ for all $i\\geq -1$.”

**Sources:**

- [Ramification groups of some finite Galois extensions of maximal nilpotency class over local fields of positive characteristic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07928v4)
- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### De Rham representations admit tensor products

**Remember:** Tensor invariant bases to get another invariant basis.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S20 (Galois theory), 14F30. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a finite extension of ℚₚ and V a finite-dimensional ℚₚ-vector space with continuous action of its absolute Galois group. Fontaine’s de Rham period field B carries a compatible action with fixed field K. Call V de Rham if extending its scalars to B gives a basis of Galois-fixed vectors.

**Problem.** Tensor products of de Rham representations are de Rham. Their spaces of fixed vectors after extension to B tensor over K.

**How the definition helps.** Tensoring two fixed bases gives a fixed basis for the tensor product (our own proof). In a fixed basis, a vector is fixed exactly when each coefficient belongs to K. This also identifies the space of periods, meaning the fixed vectors after extending scalars. The usual dimension test agrees because fixed vectors independent over K remain independent over B (our own explanation).

**nLab:** [p-adic Hodge theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/p-adic+Hodge+theory). It says: “If the dimension of V is equal to the dimension of V₍dR₎, we say that V is de Rham.”

### Cartier duals detect missing roots

**Remember:** Keep the Galois action on the roots when taking the dual.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S25 (Galois cohomology). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois module M over a p-adic field K, its Cartier dual is Hom(M,K̄×). For each σ in the absolute Galois group, define (σf)(m) = σ(f(σ⁻¹m)) (our own).

**Problem.** Let K be a p-adic field and n a positive integer. The order of H²(K, ℤ/nℤ) is the number of nth roots of unity in K.

**How the definition helps.** Evaluation at one identifies the dual of the constant module ℤ/nℤ with μₙ, respecting the Galois action (our own). Tate local duality pairs H²(K,ℤ/nℤ) perfectly with the invariant roots μₙ(K). These finite groups have the same size (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Duality for the condensed Weil-étale realisation of 1-motives over p-adic fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19910v2). It says: “Then we have a perfect cup-product pairing\\\[  \\H^ q(G<sub>F</sub>,N)\\otimes \\H^ {2-q}(G<sub>F</sub>,\\operatorname{Hom}(N,\\overline{F}<sup>\\times </sup>))\\rightarrow \\H^ 2(G<sub>F</sub>,\\overline{F}<sup>\\times </sup>)=\\mathbbm {Q}/\\mathbbm {Z}.  \\\]”

### Norm-one tori count local norms

**Remember:** Restrict scalars to the base field and take the kernel of the norm.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S25 (Galois cohomology), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite separable extension L/K, the norm-one torus T is the kernel of the norm on the restriction of scalars of the multiplicative group. In particular T(K) consists of the elements x ∈ L× with Nₗ/ₖ(x) = 1 (our own).

**Problem.** For a finite abelian extension L/K of non-Archimedean local fields, H¹(K, T) has order \[L:K\].

**How the definition helps.** The norm kernel gives an exact sequence whose first cohomology measures norm classes (our own). Hilbert’s theorem 90 and Shapiro’s lemma identify H¹(K,T) with K×/Nₗ/ₖ(L×) (our own). Local reciprocity identifies this quotient with Gal(L/K), giving its order (our own).

**nLab:** [Galois cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Galois+cohomology). It says: “Galois cohomology refers to the group cohomology of G with coefficients in a G-module naturally associated to L.”

**Wikipedia:** [Local class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_class_field_theory). It says: “the reciprocity map induces an isomorphism of the quotient group K×/N(L×)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Twisted duals make local Tate duality perfect

**Remember:** Dual into roots of unity, not into ℚ/ℤ, and the pairing becomes perfect.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S25 (Galois cohomology), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois module A over a p-adic field K, set A′ = Hom(A,μ), with μ the roots of unity in K̄. Define (σf)(a) = σ(f(σ⁻¹a)) for each Galois element σ (our own).

**Problem.** Cup product gives a perfect pairing between Hⁱ(K, A) and H²⁻ⁱ(K, A′) with values in the Brauer group ℚ/ℤ, for i = 0, 1, 2.

**How the definition helps.** The equivariant evaluation A × A′ → μ gives the cup product used by Tate local duality (our own). Over ℚ₂, the constant module ℤ/3 has three invariants, but the untwisted dual has zero second cohomology (our own). Indeed, ℚ₂ contains only one cube root of unity (our own). Tate’s theorem gives perfectness with the twisted dual (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Local Tate duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Tate_duality). It says: “It shows that the dual of such a Galois module is the Tate twist of usual linear dual.”

**Sources:**

- [Jürgen Neukirch, Alexander Schmidt and Kay Wingberg, Cohomology of Number Fields, Springer (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-37889-1)

### Unramified classes are Frobenius quotients

**Remember:** Remove inertia, then one Frobenius operator computes the group.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S25 (Galois cohomology), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let M be a finite abelian group with continuous action of the Galois group of a local field with finite residue field. Inertia is the subgroup acting trivially on the residue field. Call a first cohomology class unramified if it comes from the residue field’s Galois group acting on the inertia-fixed elements of M.

**Problem.** Write A for the inertia-fixed subgroup and F for Frobenius, the map raising residues to the residue field size. The unramified first cohomology group is A modulo the image of F − 1.

**How the definition helps.** The Galois group of the residue field is generated topologically by Frobenius, so a cocycle is fixed by its value at F (our own). Every value in A occurs, because A is finite and F acts on it through a finite cyclic quotient (our own). Changing a cocycle by a coboundary changes its value at F by an element of (F − 1)A (our own).

**nLab:** [Selmer group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Selmer+group). It says: “the unramified local condition is defined as follows:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Cup products invert swapped symbols

**Remember:** Cup the two Kummer classes and read their local invariant as a root.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a non-Archimedean local field containing all nth roots of unity, with n prime to its characteristic. For a,b ∈ K× take the cup product of their Kummer classes, with coefficients in μₙ ⊗ μₙ (our own). The local invariant identifies H²(K,μₙ ⊗ μₙ) with μₙ, giving the Hilbert symbol (a,b) (our own).

**Problem.** For all nonzero a and b in K, the Hilbert symbols (a, b) and (b, a) multiply to one.

**How the definition helps.** Cup products of degree-one classes are anticommutative, so swapping a and b negates the class (our own). The swap also exchanges the two coefficient factors, but this exchange acts trivially when the roots of unity lie in K (our own). In the group of nth roots of unity, negation is inversion (our own). The substantive step is that this symbol agrees with the one defined by local reciprocity (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_symbol). It says: “skew symmetric: (a,b) = (b,a)⁻¹”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Fundamental classes make norms commute

**Remember:** Cup with the class whose invariant is the reciprocal of the extension degree.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois extension E/K of local fields with group G, take the class in H²(G,E×) with Brauer invariant 1/\[E:K\]. Cup product with this fundamental class defines inverse reciprocity from Gᵃᵇ to K×/Nₑ/ₖ(E×) (our own).

**Problem.** Let L be intermediate between K and E. Inclusion of the two Galois groups induces a map after quotienting each group by its commutators. Under inverse reciprocity this is the norm map from L×/N(E×) to K×/N(E×), using norms from E to each base field.

**How the definition helps.** Defining inverse reciprocity by cup product makes norm compatibility an instance of the projection formula (our own). Restricting the fundamental class to the smaller Galois group gives its fundamental class. The projection formula lets the map back to the larger group pass through cup product with that class (our own). On the two sides this map gives inclusion after abelianization and the field norm (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Class formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_formation). It says: “the restriction (of cohomology classes) of a fundamental class is another fundamental class.”

**Sources:**

- [John Tate, The Higher Dimensional Cohomology Groups of Class Field Theory](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969801)
- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Lubin–Tate torsion extends cyclotomy

**Remember:** Formal group torsion supplies the unit directions that cyclotomy misses.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let O be the integer ring of a p-adic field K with uniformizer π and residue field size q. Choose a one-dimensional Lubin–Tate formal O-module whose π-series has linear term πX and reduces to Xᑫ modulo π (our own). Its division tower adjoins all points killed by πⁿ for some n ≥ 1 (our own).

**Problem.** The division tower and the maximal unramified extension together generate the maximal abelian extension of K. If \[K:ℚₚ\] exceeds one, adjoining all roots of unity of p-power order to the maximal unramified extension gives a smaller field.

**How the definition helps.** Lubin–Tate reciprocity identifies the division tower’s Galois group with O× and gives the maximal abelian extension after adjoining the maximal unramified extension. The unit group has p-adic rank \[K:ℚₚ\] (our own). The cyclotomic character has image in ℤₚ×, of rank at most one, so cyclotomy misses ramified directions when that degree exceeds one (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Théorie locale du corps de classes et (φ,Γ)-modules Lubin-Tate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13986v1). It says: “L'extension Fⁿʳ · F∞ est l'extension abélienne maximale de F”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Lubin and John Tate, Formal Complex Multiplication in Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970622)

### Lubin–Tate torsion gives abelian extensions

**Remember:** Torsion carries scalar multiplication, so Galois acts through units.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups), 11S15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let O be a complete discrete valuation ring with uniformizer π and finite residue field of size q. A Lubin–Tate formal O-module for π is a one-dimensional commutative formal O-module whose π-series reduces to Xᑫ modulo π (our own). Its π-series has linear term πX (our own).

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, adjoining all points killed by πⁿ gives a totally ramified extension, meaning its ramification index equals its degree. Its Galois group is the unit group of O modulo πⁿ, that is, (O/πⁿO)ˣ.

**How the definition helps.** Scalar multiplication puts the torsion points in a module whose automorphisms commute (our own explanation). The substantive steps prove this module is free of rank one over O/πⁿO and every unit occurs as a Galois action. A polynomial for a generating point gives the degree and total ramification (our own account).

**Wikipedia:** [Lubin–Tate formal group law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubin%E2%80%93Tate_formal_group_law). It says: “The compositum of all fields formed by adjoining such modules to the original field gives the ramified part.”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Lubin and John Tate, Formal Complex Multiplication in Local Fields (1965)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970622)

### Openness rules out false norm groups

**Remember:** A finite quotient must also be continuous to describe a class field.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a non-Archimedean local field with maximal ideal 𝔪. A subgroup H of K× is open exactly when it contains 1 + 𝔪ⁿ for some positive integer n (our own). It has finite index if K×/H is finite (our own).

**Problem.** Open subgroups of finite index in Kˣ are exactly the norm subgroups of finite abelian extensions. In positive characteristic, some subgroups of finite index are not open, so they are not norm subgroups.

**How the definition helps.** The local existence theorem identifies finite abelian norm groups with open finite-index subgroups. For K = 𝔽ₚ((t)), K×/(K×)ᵖ is an uncountable 𝔽ₚ-vector space, but its dense rational function subgroup has countable image (our own). A nonzero linear functional annihilating that image pulls back to a map onto 𝔽ₚ (our own). Its kernel is dense and proper, so it has index p but is not open (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Local class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_class_field_theory). It says: “between open subgroups of finite index in the multiplicative group”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Primitive torsion polynomials are Eisenstein

**Remember:** Removing the earlier torsion leaves an Eisenstein polynomial.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups), 11S15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a local field with uniformizer π and residue field size q, take the Lubin–Tate polynomial f(X) = πX + Xᑫ. A primitive point at level n ≥ 1 is a zero of iterate n but not iterate n−1, with iterate zero the identity (our own).

**Problem.** A primitive point of level n generates a totally ramified extension of degree (q − 1)qⁿ⁻¹.

**How the definition helps.** The quotient of iterate n by iterate n−1 is π plus the preceding iterate raised to power q−1 (our own). It is monic of degree (q−1)qⁿ⁻¹, reduces to a pure power of X, and has constant term π (our own). It is therefore Eisenstein, and adjoining any root gives a totally ramified extension of its degree (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lubin–Tate formal group law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubin%E2%80%93Tate_formal_group_law). It says: “If g is an Eisenstein polynomial, f(t) = tg(t) and F the Lubin–Tate formal group”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Lubin and John Tate, Formal Complex Multiplication in Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970622)

### Strict isomorphisms preserve division fields

**Remember:** Changing coordinates changes torsion points but not their fields.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a generator π of the maximal ideal of a non-Archimedean local field. A Lubin–Tate formal module describes addition and multiplication by integers of the field through power series. A strict isomorphism is an invertible change of coordinate over those integers with linear coefficient one that respects both operations.

**Problem.** For fixed π, every Lubin–Tate formal module generates the same field at each division level.

**How the definition helps.** For fixed π, a strict isomorphism over the integer ring carries points killed by πⁿ to points killed by πⁿ (our own). Its series converges at these points of positive valuation in their finite local fields (our own). Applying the inverse gives the opposite field inclusion, so the division fields coincide (our own). Existence of the strict isomorphism supplies the substantive input.

**Wikipedia:** [Lubin–Tate formal group law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubin%E2%80%93Tate_formal_group_law). It says: “All such group laws, for different choices of e satisfying these conditions, are strictly isomorphic.”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Lubin and John Tate, Formal Complex Multiplication in Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970622)

### Unit levels detect wild ramification

**Remember:** Level one detects wild ramification, while level zero detects inertia.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups), 11S15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite abelian extension of non-Archimedean local fields, the conductor exponent is the first unit level consisting entirely of norms. Level zero contains all units of the base field. For positive n, level n contains the units congruent to one modulo the nth power of the maximal ideal.

**Problem.** The conductor exponent is zero for unramified extensions and one for ramified tame extensions. It is at least two for wild extensions.

**How the definition helps.** Testing the first two unit levels distinguishes all three cases (our own). Local reciprocity maps the units onto inertia, the group acting trivially on the residue field (our own). It maps level one onto wild inertia, the subgroup of inertia whose order is a power of the residue characteristic (our own). The extension is unramified when inertia is trivial, and tame when wild inertia is trivial (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Conductor (class field theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_%28class_field_theory%29). It says: “Equivalently, n is the smallest integer such that the local Artin map is trivial”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Unramified norms have divisible valuations

**Remember:** Send each element to Frobenius raised to its normalized valuation.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an unramified extension of non-Archimedean local fields, define the Artin map by sending a to Frobᵛ⁽ᵃ⁾. Here v is the normalized valuation, and Frob is arithmetic Frobenius, which raises residues to the size of the base residue field.

**Problem.** In the unramified extension of degree n of a non-Archimedean local field, the norms are exactly the elements with valuation divisible by n.

**How the definition helps.** Writing the Artin image as a Frobenius power replaces a product of conjugates with a divisibility test (our own). Frobenius has order n, so its power is trivial exactly when n divides the valuation (our own). Local reciprocity identifies this kernel with the norm group (our own).

### The Weil group makes the reciprocity map an isomorphism

**Remember:** Allow only integer powers of Frobenius, and K× matches exactly.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S37 (Langlands-Weil conjectures, nonabelian class field theory), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Problem.** For a non-archimedean local field K, the reciprocity map gives an isomorphism from K× to the abelianized Weil group.

**How the definition helps.** The Weil group modulo inertia records integer Frobenius powers, matching the valuations of elements of K× (our own). Local reciprocity matches units with the inertia image and a uniformizer with a Frobenius lift in the abelianization (our own). The Weil form of local class field theory gives the isomorphism.

**Wikipedia:** [Weil group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_group). It says: “The reciprocity map of the class formation (G,A) induces an isomorphism from Aᴳ to the abelianization of the Weil group.”

### Weil characters need not be periodic

**Remember:** Discrete Frobenius powers allow arbitrary nonzero complex eigenvalues.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S37 (Langlands-Weil conjectures, nonabelian class field theory), 11S20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a local field with residue field of size q. Its Weil group consists of absolute Galois automorphisms acting on the algebraic residue field by integer powers of Frobenius, the qth power map. Inertia is the kernel of this action. Give inertia its usual topology and make it an open subgroup.

**Problem.** A complex character of the Weil group that is trivial on inertia can assign any nonzero complex number to Frobenius. It extends continuously to the absolute Galois group exactly when that number is a root of unity.

**How the definition helps.** An unramified Weil character factors through discrete ℤ, so any nonzero complex value determines it (our own). A continuous extension factors through profinite ℤ and has compact image in the unit circle (our own). The preimage of a small arc containing no nontrivial subgroup contains an open subgroup, forcing finite image (our own). Conversely, a root of unity gives a character through a finite cyclic quotient (our own).

### Brauer invariants equate period and index

**Remember:** Read the period from the denominator of the local Brauer invariant.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S45 (Algebras and orders, and their zeta functions), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The local Brauer invariant is the canonical isomorphism Br(K) → ℚ/ℤ for a non-Archimedean local field K, normalized using arithmetic Frobenius (our own). The period of a class is its order, and its index is the degree of its division algebra (our own).

**Problem.** For a central simple algebra over a non-Archimedean local field, its period equals its index.

**How the definition helps.** The local invariant turns both quantities into the denominator n of one reduced fraction (our own). The invariant identifies the Brauer group with the rationals modulo the integers, so n is the period (our own). Extending scalars to the unramified extension of degree n multiplies the invariant by n, so that extension splits the algebra (our own). The index divides every splitting degree and the period divides the index, so both equal n (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Brauer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer_group). It says: “the index of A is equal to the period of A.”

### Scalar extension multiplies Brauer invariants

**Remember:** Divide the parameter’s valuation by the unramified cyclic degree, modulo integers.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S45 (Algebras and orders, and their zeta functions), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Represent a local Brauer class by an unramified cyclic algebra with degree n, arithmetic Frobenius generator and parameter a ∈ K× (our own). The local invariant is vₖ(a)/n modulo ℤ, with vₖ normalized to take integer values (our own).

**Problem.** For any finite extension E/K of non-Archimedean local fields, the invariant of the restricted Brauer class is \[E:K\] times the original invariant.

**How the definition helps.** In the cyclic algebra formula, the invariant multiplies the parameter valuation by the unramified character’s value on Frobenius (our own). Restriction changes that value from 1/n to f/n because residue Frobenius becomes the fth power (our own). The valuation of the same parameter increases by a factor e, the ramification index (our own). Thus the multiplier is ef = \[E:K\] (our own).

### Finite differences extract Mahler coefficients

**Remember:** One difference lowers the binomial degree by one.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S80 (Other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, \\(p\\)-adic integration, etc.)). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be a continuous function from the p-adic integers ℤₚ to the p-adic numbers ℚₚ. Expand f in the binomial polynomials binom(x, n). The forward difference is Δf(x) = f(x + 1) − f(x).

**Problem.** In the Mahler expansion of f, the coefficient of binom(x, n) is the nth forward difference of f at zero.

**How the definition helps.** Pascal’s identity makes Δ send each positive-index binomial polynomial to its predecessor and sends constants to zero (our own). Mahler’s theorem supplies a uniformly convergent expansion, so each finite difference acts termwise (our own). After n differences, evaluation at zero keeps only the original term of index n (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Mahler's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_theorem). It says: “the coefficients aₙ = (Δⁿf)(0) → 0 in ℚₚ as n → ∞.”

These values come from a unique integral measure exactly when the following test holds for every finite ℂₚ-linear combination and every integer m. If the combination takes values in pᵐO, then the same combination of the assigned values lies in pᵐO.

**How the definition helps.** The functional definition turns the existence question into a bound on finite linear combinations (our own explanation). The test sends zero relations to zero and gives continuity on the span. Density and completeness then give a unique extension (our own argument).

### Trace duals locate character conductors

**Remember:** The inverse different is the largest ideal the trace character kills.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S80 (Other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, \\(p\\)-adic integration, etc.)), 11S15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L/K be a finite separable extension of non-Archimedean local fields with integer rings O<sub>L</sub> and O<sub>K</sub>. Its inverse different consists of all x ∈ L satisfying Tr(xy) ∈ O<sub>K</sub> for every y ∈ O<sub>L</sub>.

**Problem.** Let ψ be an additive character of K whose largest fractional ideal of triviality is O<sub>K</sub>. Its pullback ψ ∘ Tr is trivial on a fractional ideal of L exactly when the inverse different contains that ideal.

**How the definition helps.** The trace definition identifies the conductor directly, without computing a generator of the different (our own). The trace of a nonzero fractional ideal is a fractional ideal of K by linearity and separability (our own). The character kills this image exactly when it lies in the base integer ring (our own). Multiplying by any extension integer preserves the original ideal, so this integrality tests every pairing defining the inverse different (our own).

### Limits of powers make the Teichmüller lift multiplicative

**Remember:** Limits preserve products, and one more power shifts the sequence.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S85 (Other nonanalytic theory), 12J25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a prime p and x ∈ 𝔽ₚ, choose any p-adic integer a with residue x. Define ω(x) as the limit of the pⁿ-th powers of a as n tends to infinity (our own formulation).

**Problem.** For residues x and y modulo p, ω(xy) = ω(x)ω(y). Also, ω(x) has residue x and satisfies ω(x)ᵖ = ω(x).

**How the definition helps.** Taking limits of products gives ω(xy) = ω(x)ω(y) (our own argument). Each term has residue x, and taking pth powers shifts the sequence one place. For k ≥ 1, taking pth powers improves congruence modulo pᵏ to congruence modulo pᵏ⁺¹. Applied to successive terms or two representatives, this proves convergence and independence of the representative.

**Wikipedia:** [Teichmüller character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teichm%C3%BCller_character). It says: “If x is an integer mod p, then ω(x) is the unique solution of ω(x)ᵖ = ω(x) that is congruent to x mod p.”

### Principal units have unique prime-to-p roots

**Remember:** A principal unit has just one prime-to-p root with residue one.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S85 (Other nonanalytic theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a finite extension of the p-adic numbers, reduce each integer modulo the maximal ideal to obtain its residue. The principal units are the integers with residue one.

**Problem.** For each positive integer m prime to p, raising to the mth power is an automorphism of the principal units of a p-adic field.

**How the definition helps.** Fixing residue one excludes failures such as −1 having no square root modulo 3 (our own example). For each principal unit u, the equation xᵐ = u has root 1 in the residue field. Its derivative there is m ≠ 0, so Hensel’s lemma gives exactly one root with residue one. Thus the power homomorphism is bijective.

**Paper or page:** [Duality for condensed cohomology of the Weil group of a p-adic field](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05565v1). It says: “For m coprime to p, the continuous homomorphism (−)ᵐ: 𝒰ₖⁿ → 𝒰ₖⁿ is an isomorphism of topological groups.”

### Artin–Schreier sheaves encode lifted characters

**Remember:** A single additive cover encodes every lifted character.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽ₚ with values in ℂ. Over x ∈ k, take all solutions y of yᵖ − y = x in an algebraic closure of k. Our own function space consists of complex functions h on these solutions satisfying h(y+a) = ψ(a)h(y) for every a ∈ 𝔽ₚ.

**Problem.** For x in any finite extension k, geometric Frobenius has trace ψ(Tr(x)) on this space. Here Tr is the field trace from k to 𝔽ₚ.

**How the definition helps.** Geometric Frobenius acts on functions by precomposition with the \|k\|-power map (our own argument). Summing successive pth powers of yᵖ − y = x gives y raised to \|k\| equal to y + Tr(x). Translation thus acts by ψ(Tr(x)), and the function space has dimension one because each solution is a unique translate of any fixed solution.

### Reduced phases expose the true degree

**Remember:** Remove pth-power differences before measuring a phase.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over a finite field k of characteristic p, call two polynomial phases equivalent if their difference is gᵖ − g for some polynomial g. Replace a term a x raised to pm by b x raised to m, where bᵖ = a and m ≥ 1. Repeat after collecting terms until no positive exponent is divisible by p.

**Problem.** Fix a nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽ₚ and write Tr for the trace to 𝔽ₚ. Equivalent phases give equal sums S(f) = ∑ₓ ψ(Tr(f(x))), where x ranges over k. If the reduced phase has degree d ≥ 1, then \|S(f)\| ≤ (d − 1)√\|k\|.

**How the definition helps.** Reduction measures the degree only after discarding differences invisible to the field trace. Our own calculation uses Tr(gᵖ) = Tr(g) at every input. The Weil bound applies because the remaining degree is prime to p. For example, xᵖ − x reduces to zero and its sum equals \|k\|.

**nLab:** [Artin-Schreier sequence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Artin-Schreier+sequence). It says: “There is a short exact sequence of abelian sheaves over the étale site”

### Smooth top forms give Deligne cancellation

**Remember:** Test the highest-degree terms on projective space.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take a polynomial f of degree d ≥ 2 in m ≥ 2 variables over 𝔽𝓆. Assume the characteristic does not divide d. Call f smooth at infinity if its degree-d part and all its first partial derivatives have no common nonzero zero over the algebraic closure.

**Problem.** Let ψ be a nontrivial additive character and let f be smooth at infinity. Then the sum of ψ(f(x)) over all x in 𝔽𝓆ᵐ has modulus at most (d − 1)ᵐ√(qᵐ).

**How the definition helps.** Testing only the top form excludes flat directions that can make a multivariable sum too large. Our own example in odd characteristic is f(x) = x₁². Each of the other variables multiplies the quadratic Gauss sum by q, giving modulus qᵐ/√q. Deligne’s theorem supplies the bound under the smoothness condition.

### Unique shifts force Burgess cancellation

**Remember:** A shift used once gives a zero or pole of order one.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 11L40. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Problem.** For each x modulo p, multiply χ(x + b) over the first r shifts b and its complex conjugate over the last r. For a nonexceptional list, the sum of these products over x has modulus at most 2r√p.

**How the definition helps.** A shift that appears once gives a simple zero or pole of the quotient of the two products of linear factors. So the quotient is not a power of degree equal to the order of χ (our own explanation). The character bound in Corollary 11.24 of Iwaniec and Kowalski then applies, including at the excluded zeros. Repeating the first half as the second gives p minus the number of distinct shifts.

### Negative Gauss sums lift multiplicatively

**Remember:** Negating each Gauss sum absorbs the sign in the lifting formula.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11T24 (Other character sums and Gauss sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A multiplicative character χ sends products to products, and an additive character ψ sends sums to products of complex numbers of absolute value one. Define the signed Gauss sum as the negative of the sum of χ(x)ψ(x) over nonzero field elements. Over an extension, evaluate χ on the norm, the product of conjugates, and ψ on the trace, their sum.

**Problem.** For nontrivial characters over a finite field, the signed sum over an extension of degree n equals the nth power of the signed base sum.

**How the definition helps.** In our own normalization, taking the negative absorbs the alternating sign in the Davenport–Hasse lifting theorem. That theorem supplies the relation between fields for the ordinary Gauss sums. Multiplying its formula by −1 gives precisely the nth power of the signed base sum.

**Paper or page:** [Davenport and Hasse's theorems and lifts of multiplication matrices of Gaussian periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14872). It says: “Then, for any integer n ≥ 1, we have Gₙᵣ(ψ′) = (−1)ⁿ⁻¹Gᵣ(ψ)ⁿ”

### Nonpowers give Kummer cancellation

**Remember:** A perfect power makes the character constant away from its zeros and poles.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11T24 (Other character sums and Gauss sums), 11T23, 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let k be a finite field and d &gt; 1. A nonzero f ∈ k(x) is a geometric dth power if f = gᵈ for some rational function g over the algebraic closure.

**Problem.** Let χ have order d on the multiplicative group of k, where \|k\| = q. Unless f is a geometric dth power, summing χ(f(x)) over finite k-points outside its zeros and poles gives modulus at most (s − 2)√q. Here s counts infinity and all distinct finite zeros and poles over the algebraic closure.

**How the definition helps.** Our own explanation uses the orders of zeros and poles to test whether the character can stay constant. On the projective line, f is a geometric dth power exactly when d divides every such order. For f(x) = xᵈ, every nonzero input contributes one. The Weil bound for multiplicative character sums supplies the estimate in the other case.

### Diophantine sets with parameters let Hilbert's tenth problem meet computability

**Remember:** A tuple belongs exactly when its equation has a witness.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11U05 (Decidability (number-theoretic aspects)), 03D25. arXiv math.NT, math.LO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A set S of tuples of natural numbers is Diophantine if one polynomial p(a, x) with integer coefficients describes it. Namely, a is in S exactly when p(a, x) = 0 has a solution x in natural numbers.

**Problem.** Every computably enumerable set is Diophantine (the MRDP theorem). Hence no algorithm decides whether an integer polynomial has an integer root tuple.

**How the definition helps.** The parameters index a family of equations, so their solvable instances form a set (our own explanation). MRDP represents a noncomputable enumerable set this way. A decision procedure over the integers would decide membership, since Lagrange’s four-square theorem represents every natural-number unknown by four integer squares.

### Continued fractions with minus signs make the half-line a terminal coalgebra

**Remember:** Always round strictly up, so every number has only one expansion.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A55 (Continued fractions), 18C40. arXiv math.NT, math.CT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For x ≥ 1, let β(x) be the least integer strictly greater than x. Define ξ(x) = (β(x), 1/(β(x) − x)).

**Problem.** With the lexicographic order, (ℝ≥1, ξ) is the terminal coalgebra of the functor X ↦ ℕ≥2 × X on linear orders. So a real number x ≥ 1 is the same thing as its infinite stream of digits.

**How the definition helps.** Each digit a ≥ 2 gives an increasing inverse branch t ↦ a − 1/t (our own proof). For a fixed prefix of n digits, the possible values form a half-open interval of length at most 1/n by the continued-fraction recurrence. Each infinite tail starts with a finite digit, keeping its value below the excluded upper endpoint. Thus streams determine unique values in lexicographic order, and iterating any coalgebra gives its unique map to streams.
