**Remember:** Intersect the sets in two cut tests to get another cut test.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For fixed r≥2, test f on ℤ/Nℤ by averaging f(x₁+⋯+xᵣ) times a product of r indicators over independent uniform inputs. The i-th indicator tests an arbitrary subset of all coordinates except xᵢ. The arithmetic cut norm is the supremum of the absolute values of these averages.

**Problem.** For every ε &gt; 0 there is an η &gt; 0, independent of N, with this property. Suppose ν ≥ 0, the cut norm of ν − 1 is at most η, and 0 ≤ f ≤ ν. Then some function g with values in \[0,1\] makes the cut norm of f − g at most ε.

**How the definition helps.** The product of two cut tests is another cut test because their indicators multiply by intersecting sets (our own explanation). The dense model theorem uses convex separation to test whether a bounded approximation exists. Polynomial approximation reduces the separating test to products that the cut norm already controls.

**Wikipedia:** [Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem). It says: “A more general relative Szemerédi theorem has since been given by David Conlon, Jacob Fox, and Yufei Zhao.”

**Sources:**

- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, The Green–Tao theorem: an exposition, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 1 (2014), 249–282](https://doi.org/10.4171/emss/6)

### Entropic doubling contracts under homomorphisms

**Remember:** Measure doubling with entropy, and homomorphisms can only shrink it.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity), 11B13, 94A17. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For independent finitely supported X,Y in an abelian group, define their entropic distance as H(X−Y) − (H(X)+H(Y))/2. Here H is Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. Entropic doubling is exp(H(X+X′)−H(X)) for an independent copy X′ (our own formulation).

**Problem.** Entropic doubling cannot increase under a group homomorphism π. For independent X,Y, their entropic distance is at least the distance between πX,πY plus the mean distance between their conditional laws on the corresponding fibres.

**How the definition helps.** Proposition 1.4 bounds the distance below by the image distance plus the mean distance between conditional laws on the two fibres. The fibre distances are nonnegative because conditioning on either summand shows that the difference entropy dominates each individual entropy. Applying this to X and −X′ gives contraction of doubling (our own argument).

**Paper or page:** [Sumsets and entropy revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13403), [Sumsets and entropy revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13403). It says: “it enjoys somewhat better properties; for instance, it contracts upon applying a homomorphism.”

**Sources:**

- [Ben Green, Freddie Manners, Terence Tao, Sumsets and entropy revisited, Random Struct. Alg. (2024) 1-33, arXiv:2306.13403](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13403)

### Finite complexity separates binary prime problems

**Remember:** A parallel pair cannot be separated into any allowed classes.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take fixed nonconstant affine forms with integer coefficients, and write vᵢ for the coefficient vector of the linear part of form i. For each i, partition the remaining vectors into at most s+1 classes whose rational spans all exclude vᵢ. The complexity is the least nonnegative s that works for every i, or infinity if none works.

**Problem.** Let K ⊆ \[−N,N\]ᵈ be convex with all t fixed forms positive on K. For finite complexity, the sum of ∏ᵢ Λ(ψᵢ(n)) over lattice points in K equals vol(K)∏ₚβₚ + o(Nᵈ). Here Λ is the von Mangoldt function, and βₚ equals the fraction of residues n avoiding all zeros modulo p divided by (1−1/p)ᵗ.

**How the definition helps.** The partition condition identifies systems covered by the counting theorem and excludes pairs with proportional slopes (our own explanation). If no slopes are proportional, singleton classes suffice. The forms n and n+2 share a slope, so the theorem makes no claim about twin primes. The asymptotic requires Green and Tao’s prime counting theorem and the later results that establish its hypotheses.

**Paper or page:** [Improved quadratic Gowers uniformity for the Möbius function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09635). It says: “Let Ψ be affine forms such that no two ψᵢ differ by a constant.”

**Sources:**

- [Green and Tao, Linear equations in primes, Annals of Mathematics 171 (2010), 1753–1850](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2010.171.1753)
- [Green, Tao and Ziegler, An inverse theorem for the Gowers Uˢ⁺¹\[N\] norm, Annals of Mathematics 176 (2012), 1231–1372](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2012.176.2.11)
- [Green and Tao, The Möbius function is strongly orthogonal to nilsequences, Annals of Mathematics 175 (2012), 541–566](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2012.175.2.3)

### Linear forms tests transfer Szemerédi's theorem

**Remember:** Test the doubled patterns that appear in the counting proof.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix k ≥ 3 and sample two independent uniform residues for each of k coordinates modulo a prime N, all choices independent. For each j from 1 to k, form every sum Σᵢ≠ⱼ(j−i)zᵢ using either residue at each coordinate i ≠ j. Evaluate the nonnegative weight ν on each indexed sum. The k-linear forms condition requires the mean of every subproduct to approach one as N grows.

**Problem.** Suppose ν satisfies this condition, 0 ≤ f ≤ ν, and the mean of f is at least δ &gt; 0. The mean of f(x)⋯f(x+(k−1)d) over uniform x,d is at least c(k,δ)−o(1), with c(k,δ)&gt;0.

**How the definition helps.** The tests control the extra products created when Cauchy–Schwarz duplicates an input (our own explanation). Conlon, Fox and Zhao compare the progression count with that of a bounded function with similar mean. The dense form of Szemerédi’s theorem supplies a positive lower bound for that function.

**Wikipedia:** [Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem). It says: “It is not implied by Szemerédi's theorem because the primes have density 0 in the natural numbers.”

**Sources:**

- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, A relative Szemerédi theorem, Geometric and Functional Analysis 25 (2015), 733–762](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-015-0324-9)
- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, The Green–Tao theorem: an exposition, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 1 (2014), 249–282](https://doi.org/10.4171/emss/6)

### Local factors count prime progressions

**Remember:** Separate real volume from each prime’s divisibility correction.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity), 11N13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix k ≥ 3 and count pairs (x,d) modulo p for which none of x,x+d,…,x+(k−1)d vanishes. Divide their fraction by (1−1/p)ᵏ to obtain βₚ. The singular series is the product of βₚ over primes p.

**Problem.** For fixed k≥3, the count of strictly increasing k-term prime progressions at most N is asymptotic to N²∏ₚβₚ divided by 2(k−1)(log N)ᵏ.

**How the definition helps.** The singular series collects the local divisibility corrections (our own calculation). For p ≤ k only d = 0 works, giving p−1 pairs. For p &gt; k each nonzero d forbids k starts, giving (p−1)(p−k+1) pairs overall. The Green–Tao counting theorem gives the asymptotic with leading area N²/(2(k−1)).

**Wikipedia:** [Green–Tao theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Tao_theorem). It says: “for the number of k tuples of primes p₁ &lt; p₂ &lt; ⋯ &lt; pₖ ≤ N in arithmetic progression.”

**Sources:**

- [Green and Tao, Linear equations in primes, Annals of Mathematics 171 (2010), 1753–1850](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2010.171.1753)
- [Green, Tao and Ziegler, An inverse theorem for the Gowers Uˢ⁺¹\[N\] norm, Annals of Mathematics 176 (2012), 1231–1372](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2012.176.2.11)
- [Green and Tao, The Möbius function is strongly orthogonal to nilsequences, Annals of Mathematics 175 (2012), 541–566](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2012.175.2.3)

### Minimum quadratic rank gives uniform fibers

**Remember:** Check every combination, because two high-rank quadratics can cancel.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let Q comprise d quadratic polynomials on a finite vector space H over a field of odd prime order p. For a quadratic part q, its rank is the matrix rank of the bilinear form q(x+y)−q(x)−q(y). The tuple rank is the minimum rank among combinations whose coefficients are not all zero.

**Problem.** If Q has rank at least R, each equation Q(x)=b has \|H\|p⁻ᵈ solutions up to an error of at most \|H\|/√(pᴿ).

**How the definition helps.** Testing all combinations controls every oscillating term in the Fourier expansion of the solution count (our own explanation). For example, the pair (q,q) never takes a value with unequal coordinates, however large the rank of q. The quadratic exponential sum estimate bounds each nonconstant term by the reciprocal of √(pᴿ) after averaging over H. Subtracting b reduces any target to the quoted zero count.

**Paper or page:** [An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³-norm relative to quadratic level sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07962). It says: “be a d-tuple of quadratic polynomials on H of rank at least R.”

**Sources:**

- [Sean Prendiville, An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³-norm relative to quadratic level sets, arXiv:2409.07962v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07962)

### Normal form exposes the counting bound

**Remember:** Each rival form misses a coordinate that the chosen form uses.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A system of nonzero linear forms over 𝔽ₚ is in s-normal form if each form admits the following coordinate selection. Select at most s+1 coordinates it uses, so every other form omits at least one selected coordinate.

**Problem.** Evaluate all forms on the same tuple of independent uniform inputs from a finite 𝔽ₚ-vector space. Let Λ(f₁,…,fₜ) average the product of the fᵢ evaluated on their respective forms. For \[0,1\]-valued fᵢ,gᵢ, the change on replacing all fᵢ by gᵢ has modulus at most the sum of the order-(s+1) Gowers norms of fᵢ−gᵢ.

**How the definition helps.** The selected coordinates specify which variables to duplicate in Cauchy–Schwarz (our own explanation). Each competing factor disappears at a step involving a coordinate it omits. What remains is a Gowers norm, which measures an alternating product over the vertices of an additive cube. The counting lemma gives the bound for one replacement, and adding the bounds covers all replacements.

**Paper or page:** [Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463). It says: “Let Φ : Gᵏ → Gᵐ be a system of linear forms in s-normal form, and suppose that Φ is coprime.”

**Sources:**

- [Davi Castro-Silva, Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs, arXiv:2107.01463v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463)

### Power dependence defeats lower-order counting

**Remember:** A relation among powers makes the phases cancel in the product.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix linear forms ψ₁,…,ψₜ over 𝔽ₚ with p &gt; d ≥ 2. Their dth powers are dependent if ∑ᵢ aᵢψᵢᵈ vanishes as a polynomial for some nonzero coefficient vector over 𝔽ₚ.

**Problem.** Apply each form coordinatewise to vectors in 𝔽ₚⁿ. If their dth powers are dependent, some unit-modulus functions fᵢ have product one along the forms at every input. At least one fᵢ has order-d Gowers norm tending to zero as n grows.

**How the definition helps.** A dependence relation supplies cancelling phases (our own example). At x ∈ 𝔽ₚⁿ take fᵢ(x) = exp(2πi aᵢ∑ⱼ xⱼᵈ/p), interpreting field elements modulo p. For aᵢ ≠ 0, the d-fold difference in each coordinate has exponent proportional to aᵢd!h₁⋯h<sub>d</sub>, giving a nonconstant unit phase. Its mean has modulus below one, and independence raises that modulus to the nth power in the Gowers norm calculation.

**Paper or page:** [On a conjecture of Gowers and Wolf](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15437). It says: “the polynomials ψ₁ˢ⁺¹, …, ψₜˢ⁺¹ are linearly independent.”

**Sources:**

- [Daniel Altman, On a conjecture of Gowers and Wolf, arXiv:2106.15437v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15437)

### Relative density reaches sparse prime subsets

**Remember:** Compare a set of primes with the primes themselves.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let π(N) count primes at most N. For a set A of primes, use the upper relative density limsup as N → ∞ of \|A ∩ \[1,N\]\|/π(N). This uses the primes as the reference set instead of all integers.

**Problem.** Every set of primes with positive upper relative density contains infinitely many nonconstant arithmetic progressions of each fixed length k ≥ 2.

**How the definition helps.** Relative density gives a prime subset a positive share even when its density among integers is zero (our own explanation). Green and Tao prove that Szemerédi’s progression theorem extends to sets bounded by suitable weights. A sieve supplies such a weight for the primes.

**Wikipedia:** [Green–Tao theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Tao_theorem). It says: “the set A contains infinitely many arithmetic progressions of length k.”

**Sources:**

- [Green and Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Annals of Mathematics 167 (2008), 481–547](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2008.167.481)

### Rough weights make prime uniformity measurable

**Remember:** Compare primes with integers that avoid the same small prime divisors.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let P be the product of primes below w, and let φ(P) count residues coprime to P. The Cramér model M assigns P/φ(P) to integers coprime to P and zero elsewhere. Its mean over a period equals one.

**Problem.** Take w=exp((log N)¹ᐟ¹⁰) and fixed k ≥ 2. On \[1,N\], the order-k Gowers norm of Λ−M is O((log log N)⁻ᶜ) for some c=c(k)&gt;0. This norm averages products over additive cubes, and Λ gives weight log p to positive powers of p and zero elsewhere.

**How the definition helps.** The model preserves the small-prime biases that prevent the constant function from approximating Λ (our own explanation). For example, the mean of (Λ(n)−1)exp(2πin/3) tends to −1/2 by the prime number theorem in residue classes. Tao and Teräväinen’s quantitative uniformity theorem bounds the remaining cube averages.

**Paper or page:** [Improved quadratic Gowers uniformity for the Möbius function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09635). It says: “\\\|\\Lambda - \\Lambda <sub>Q</sub>\\\| <sub>U<sup>s</sup>(\[N\])</sub> \\ll (\\log \\log (N))<sup>-c</sup>”

**Sources:**

- [Tao and Teräväinen, Quantitative bounds for Gowers uniformity of the Möbius and von Mangoldt functions, JEMS 27 (2025), 1321–1384](https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1404)

### Squared sieve weights dominate primes

**Remember:** Beyond the divisor cutoff, a prime contributes only its divisor one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity), 11N13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Choose smooth χ supported on \[−1,1\], with 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1 and χ(0)=1. Define S(m) by summing μ(d)χ(log d/log R) over divisors d of m, using the Möbius function μ. Let W be the product of primes up to w and c the integral of \|χ′\|² over \[0,1\]. On residues N/2 ≤ n &lt; N use ν(n)=φ(W)log(R)S(Wn+1)²/(Wc), and use one elsewhere.

**Problem.** Fix k ≥ 3, let N run through large primes, choose w growing sufficiently slowly, and set a = 1/(8k·2ᵏ), R = Nᵃ. Then ν passes the k-linear forms test, meaning every subproduct on the doubled progression forms has mean 1+o(1). At primes Wn+1 in the specified half, ν(n) is at least (a/2c)(φ(W)/W)log(Wn+1).

**How the definition helps.** Squaring the divisor sum makes the weight nonnegative while preserving its size at large primes (our own explanation). At primes above R only the divisor one contributes, so S equals one. Since log(Wn+1) ≤ 2 log N for large N, this gives the stated lower bound. Proposition 8.3 of the cited exposition estimates products of divisor sums to prove the linear forms condition.

**Wikipedia:** [Green–Tao theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Tao_theorem). It says: “To construct this set, Green and Tao used ideas from Goldston, Pintz, and Yıldırım's work on prime gaps.”

**Sources:**

- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, The Green–Tao theorem: an exposition, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 1 (2014), 249–282](https://doi.org/10.4171/emss/6)
- [Green and Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Annals of Mathematics 167 (2008), 481–547](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2008.167.481)

### Unique square completion turns a 1-step nilspace into an abelian group

**Remember:** Fix an origin, then the fourth corner of a square is the sum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.CO, math.DS. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a nonempty set X, nilspace cubes include all pairs and admit precomposition by affine integer maps between discrete cubes. Every corner missing the all-ones vertex extends if each face avoiding that vertex is a cube. A 1-step nilspace requires exactly one extension for every square corner.

**Problem.** Every 1-step nilspace X admits a free transitive action of an abelian group A. Its cubes are exactly the maps ω ↦ x+∑ᵢωᵢhᵢ for x ∈ X and increments hᵢ ∈ A.

**How the definition helps.** Choose an origin o and define x+y as the missing vertex opposite o in the square with adjacent vertices x,y (our own explanation). The structure theorem for 1-step nilspaces proves the group laws and identifies every higher cube with an affine cube of this group.

**Paper or page:** [Notes on nilspaces: algebraic aspects](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03693v3). It says: “Then there is an abelian group A such that 𝒩 is a principal homogeneous space of A and the cubes on 𝒩 are the projections of the degree-1 cubes on A.”

**Sources:**

- [Pablo Candela, Notes on nilspaces: algebraic aspects, arXiv:1601.03693 (2017). Discrete Analysis, 2017:15, 59pp](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03693v3)

### Weighted deletion extends arithmetic removal

**Remember:** Delete little weight, even when the support has tiny density.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Deleting B from a nonnegative function f on ℤ/Nℤ costs the sum of f(x) over x ∈ B divided by N. The weighted progression count averages ∏ⱼ fⱼ(x+(j−1)d) over uniform independent x,d.

**Problem.** Fix k ≥ 3 and ε &gt; 0, and assume N is sufficiently large and prime. Suppose 0 ≤ fᵢ ≤ ν and ν satisfies the k-linear forms condition. Below some positive count threshold c(k,ε), each fᵢ admits a deletion costing at most ε, collectively removing every progression from the ordered supports.

**How the definition helps.** Weighted deletion measures the mass that actually contributes to the count, even when the support occupies few residues (our own explanation). Conlon, Fox and Zhao’s relative arithmetic removal lemma gives the deletions. Its proof represents progressions by overlapping coordinate sets and applies the weighted removal theorem to those sets.

**Paper or page:** [The Green-Tao theorem for affine curves over 𝔽(q)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00839). It says: “Then there is a family of subsets”

**Sources:**

- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, A relative Szemerédi theorem, Geometric and Functional Analysis 25 (2015), 733–762](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-015-0324-9)

### Sidon sets give error-correcting codes

**Remember:** Repeated pair sums are exactly the short column relations that spoil the code.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B75 (Other combinatorial number theory), 94B05. arXiv math.CO, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a binary vector space, a set is Sidon if distinct unordered pairs of distinct elements have different sums.

**Problem.** Let n &gt; t ≥ 2. A Sidon set of size n + 1 exists in the t-dimensional binary vector space exactly when a certain binary linear code exists. The code has length n, dimension n − t, and no nonzero word with fewer than five nonzero coordinates.

**How the definition helps.** Translate the set to contain zero and use its other elements as matrix columns (our own proof). Distinct nonzero columns exclude dependencies of sizes one and two, while Sidon excludes sizes three and four by pairing with zero if needed. The kernel has dimension at least n−t, so it contains a code of the required dimension. Conversely, a parity-check matrix of the stated code has t independent rows and its columns satisfy precisely these restrictions.

**Paper or page:** [Sidon sets, sum-free sets and linear codes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07906v3). It says: “There is no Sidon set M ⊆ 𝔽₂ᵗ of size n + 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Sidon sets, sum-free sets and linear codes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07906v3)

### Oriented quadratic algebras let twisted binary forms describe Picard groups

**Remember:** Orient the algebra first, then the form classes give its ideal classes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms), 11R65, 14F06. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let A be a quadratic algebra, locally free of rank two over a scheme S, and let N be a line bundle. An N-orientation of A is an isomorphism from A modulo the scalar submodule to the dual line bundle of N.

**Problem.** Fix a scheme on which 2 is not a zero divisor and a line bundle N. Fix discriminant and parity arising from an N-oriented quadratic algebra. The classes of primitive N-twisted binary quadratic forms with these invariants correspond to the Picard group of that oriented algebra.

**How the definition helps.** The orientation keeps track of the algebra when the quotient by scalars has no global basis. The paper shows that the discriminant and the parity classify the oriented algebras. The paper says that Wood's earlier bijection needs this refinement to give Picard groups.

**Paper or page:** [Recovering the Picard group of quadratic algebras from Wood's binary quadratic forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.13422v5). It says: “Extending the notion of orientation of quadratic algebras to the non-free case is another key step, eventually leading us to the desired parametrization.”

**Sources:**

- [William Dallaporta, Recovering the Picard group of quadratic algebras from Wood's binary quadratic forms, arXiv:2111.13422v5 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.13422v5)

### Primitive values distinguish binary forms

**Remember:** Use coprime inputs to tell primitive forms apart.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A binary quadratic form is a polynomial ax² + bxy + cy². An integral form is primitive if its coefficients have greatest common divisor one. Its primitive values come from integer pairs with coprime coordinates. Its discriminant is b² − 4ac.

**Problem.** Primitive integral binary quadratic forms with nonsquare discriminants are equivalent if they have the same primitive values. Equivalence means an invertible integer change of variables.

**How the definition helps.** Coprime inputs distinguish two inequivalent forms that represent the same integers when all inputs count (our own). The forms x² + xy + y² and x² + 3y² have the same ordinary values but different discriminants. The first represents 4 only when both coordinates are even, while the second gives 4 at (1,1) (our own). Fouvry and Koymans prove that equal primitive value sets force equivalence.

**Paper or page:** [Binary quadratic forms with the same value set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09575v2), [Binary quadratic forms with the same value set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09575v2). It says: “Let F and G be two primitive quadratic forms, with non square discriminants and with F(ℤ²ₚᵣᵢₘ) = G(ℤ²ₚᵣᵢₘ).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Forms with integer matrix need only 1 to 15 to be universal

**Remember:** Integer matrix means even cross terms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11E12. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An integral quadratic form has integer matrix if, in integral coordinates, its symmetric coefficient matrix has integer entries. Equivalently, every mixed term has even coefficient.

**Problem.** If a positive definite quadratic form with integer matrix represents every integer from 1 through 15, it represents every positive integer.

**How the definition helps.** The matrix condition specifies exactly the class addressed by the Conway–Schneeberger 15 theorem (our own explanation). That theorem supplies the finite test for universality.

**Wikipedia:** [15 and 290 theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_and_290_theorems). It says: “The 15 theorem says that a quadratic form with integer matrix is universal if it takes the numbers from 1 to 15 as values.”

**Sources:**

- [M. Bhargava, On the Conway–Schneeberger fifteen theorem, in Quadratic Forms and Their Applications (Dublin, 1999), Contemporary Mathematics (2000)](http://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~aar/books/dublin.pdf)

### Weighting forms with extra symmetry gives Hurwitz class numbers modular behaviour

**Remember:** Count the square and hexagonal forms fractionally, and generating functions become modular.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E41 (Class numbers of quadratic and Hermitian forms), 11F37. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For N &gt; 0, sum over SL₂(ℤ)-classes of positive definite integral binary quadratic forms of discriminant −N, including imprimitive forms. Each class contributes 2 divided by the order of its stabilizer in SL₂(ℤ). This sum defines H(N), and H(0) = −1/12.

**Problem.** With these weights, the generating function Σ H(N) qᴺ is a mock modular form of weight 3/2. That is, Zagier showed that adding a simple correction term makes it transform like a modular form of weight 3/2.

**How the definition helps.** The stabilizer weights account for extra symmetries in the modular generating series (our own explanation). The square and hexagonal forms have stabilizers of orders four and six, hence weights one half and one third. Zagier’s theorem supplies the nonholomorphic correction and the weight-3/2 transformation law.

**Wikipedia:** [Hurwitz class number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz_class_number). It says: “forms are weighted by 2/g for g the order of their automorphism group, and where H(0) = –1/12.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Weighting lattices by one over their symmetries gives the mass formula

**Remember:** Count each lattice as one over its symmetries, and the total is computable.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E41 (Class numbers of quadratic and Hermitian forms), 11E08. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Two positive definite integral quadratic forms are in the same genus when they are equivalent over the p-adic integers for every prime p (our own). The mass of a genus is Σ 1/\|Aut(Λ)\| over its classes Λ. Here Aut(Λ) is the finite group of symmetries of the lattice.

**Problem.** For dimension n ≥ 2, the mass of a genus equals an explicit product of local factors, one for each prime.

**How the definition helps.** The reciprocal automorphism weights express mass as a volume (our own explanation). The Smith–Minkowski–Siegel mass formula factors this volume into local contributions with the real normalization for the dimension and determinant.

**Wikipedia:** [Smith–Minkowski–Siegel mass formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith%E2%80%93Minkowski%E2%80%93Siegel_mass_formula). It says: “a formula for the sum of the weights of the lattices (quadratic forms) in a genus, weighted by the reciprocals of the orders of their automorphism groups.”

### Relative completion retains modular monodromy

**Remember:** Keep the reductive quotient before completing.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F06 (Structure of modular groups and generalizations; arithmetic groups), 20G30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a Zariski-dense homomorphism from a group Γ to a reductive algebraic group R over ℚ. Its relative completion is the inverse limit of algebraic extensions of R by unipotent groups equipped with a Zariski-dense lift of Γ. Taking R trivial gives ordinary rational unipotent completion (our own formulation).

**Problem.** The ordinary rational unipotent completion of the modular group SL₂(ℤ) is trivial. Its completion relative to the standard inclusion surjects onto the algebraic group SL₂ over ℚ.

**How the definition helps.** The dense inclusion gives a completion surjecting onto SL₂ by construction (our own argument). Integer elementary matrices are dense in each elementary one-parameter subgroup, and these subgroups generate SL₂. The finite abelianization of SL₂(ℤ) rules out nonzero rational additive characters. Any nontrivial unipotent image would supply such a character through its Zariski closure.

**nLab:** [Malcev completion](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Malcev+completion). It says: “Mal'cev completion is a left adjoint functor to the embedding of the category of uniquely divisible nilpotent groups into the category of nilpotent groups.”

**Sources:**

- [Richard Hain, The Hodge-de Rham Theory of Modular Groups](https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781316387887.019)

### Big theta quotients detect pairs

**Remember:** Take the largest quotient with the desired first action.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F27 (Theta series; Weil representation; theta correspondences), 11F70. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take an orthogonal–symplectic dual pair over a p-adic field of odd residue characteristic, using the covering groups required by the Weil representation. For irreducible smooth complex π of the first group, take the largest quotient on which that group acts by copies of π. The big theta lift Θ(π) is the second group’s representation on the multiplicity space in this quotient π ⊗ Θ(π).

**Problem.** Take an irreducible smooth complex representation σ of the second group. The Weil representation surjects onto π tensored with σ exactly when Θ(π) surjects onto σ. Such a σ is unique up to isomorphism and is called the small theta lift.

**How the definition helps.** The largest quotient collects all maps onto pairs with first factor π in a single representation (our own). Its defining property reduces testing each pair separately to testing quotients of Θ(π) (our own). Howe duality proves the further assertion that a nonzero big lift has a unique irreducible quotient.

**Paper or page:** [Equal rank local theta correspondence as a strong Morita equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.13484v3). It says: “Θ(π) is either zero or has a unique irreducible quotient, so that θ(π) is irreducible.”

**Sources:**

- [Wee Teck Gan and Shuichiro Takeda, A proof of the Howe duality conjecture](https://doi.org/10.1090/jams/839)

### A three-block product excludes exceptional zeros

**Remember:** Four copies of a real zero overwhelm three poles.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let π be a unitary cuspidal representation distinct from its dual π̃, with central character trivial on positive real scalars. Form the list Π = (1,π,π̃), where 1 is the trivial character. Define D(s) by multiplying the nine Rankin–Selberg functions pairing this list with its dual list.

**Problem.** For fixed rank and number field, some effective c &gt; 0 excludes real zeros of L(s,π) in \[1−c/log(3+C),1). The analytic conductor C combines the finite conductor and the sizes of the gamma factors at height zero.

**How the definition helps.** The auxiliary product has four copies of any real zero but only three poles at one (our own explanation). Two factors are L(s,π), and two are its complex conjugate along the real axis. Only the matched dual pairs contribute poles. Positivity for −D′/D and conductor bounds for the nine factors permit at most three zeros in the stated interval, counted with multiplicity.

**Paper or page:** [Exceptional zeros of Rankin-Selberg L-functions and joint Sato-Tate distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06482v2). It says: “is not self-dual, then L(s,π) has no exceptional zero.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Abelian quotient isolates zero-free factors

**Remember:** Remove the scalar line before bounding the other factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a full-level holomorphic cuspidal Hecke eigenform, let π denote its normalized representation and C its analytic conductor. For each m ≥ 1, remove the scalar factor from the symmetric-power Rankin–Selberg function by setting R(s) = L(s,Symᵐπ × Symᵐπ)/ζ(s).

**Problem.** There is an absolute, effectively computable c &gt; 0 such that R(s) has no real zeros for s ≥ 1−c/(m² log(3mC²)).

**How the definition helps.** Dividing by ζ(s) removes the scalar factor from the self-pairing (our own specialization). The cited zero-free theorem applies because full-level forms have trivial central character and no complex multiplication.

**Paper or page:** [Exceptional zeros of Rankin-Selberg L-functions and joint Sato-Tate distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06482v2). It says: “There exists an absolute, effectively computable constant”

**Sources:**

### Additive twists encode modular transformations

**Remember:** A rational additive twist records the cusp used in a transformation.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an absolutely convergent Dirichlet series on Re s &gt; 1, its completed additive twist at rational x is T(s,x) = γ(s)∑ₙ a(n)exp(2πinx)/nˢ. Take γ(s) = Qˢ∏Γ(λs+μ), with Q,λ positive, ∑λ = 1 and Re μ &gt; −λ/2 for each factor.

**Problem.** Fix positive integral N, a character χ modulo N and ω ≠ 0. For every positive multiple q of N and ab ≡ 1 modulo q, assume both twists in T(s,a/q)=ωχ(b)q¹⁻²ˢT(1−s,−b/q) are entire of finite order. Then for some positive integer k, the coefficients a(n)n⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾ᐟ² give a modular Fourier series of weight k, level N and character χ.

**How the definition helps.** The additive phase identifies the two rational shifts that a modular transformation relates. In our own explanation, the factor e(nx) translates the nth Fourier term by x. The converse theorem recovers modular symmetry from the paired functional equations. Identifying the gamma factor and inverting the Mellin transform supply the analytic work.

**Paper or page:** [An extension of Venkatesh's converse theorem to the Selberg class](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00451v1). It says: “Given any α ∈ ℚ, define the complete twisted L-function”

### Analytic conductor measures sum length

**Remember:** The square root of the conductor sets the central sum length.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f,g be level-one Hecke–Maass cusp forms with normalized Hecke eigenvalues λf(n),λg(n). The central analytic conductor of L(s,f×g) equals its finite conductor times ∏κ(3+\|κ\|), indexed by its gamma factors Γℝ(s+κ).

**Problem.** For Q &gt; 1 and ε &gt; 0, some smooth W depending only on Q,ε vanishes beyond Q raised to ½+ε. Put S(t) = the sum of λf(n)λg(n)W(n) divided by n raised to ½+it over all n ≥ 1. For every pair with C ≤ Q, \|L(½,f×g)\|² ≪ Qᵋ∫\|S(t)\|²dt + Q⁻¹⁰⁰, integrating over \|t\| ≤ log Q.

**How the definition helps.** The conductor gives one cutoff for every pair with C ≤ Q, so the cited lemma can choose W using only Q and ε. In our own explanation, estimates for the gamma factors in the functional equation give the square-root scale.

**Paper or page:** [Uniform subconvexity bounds for GL(2) × GL(2) L-functions in the spectral aspect](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05968v1). It says: “Then there exists a function W(x) depending on Q and ε only”

**Sources:**

### Dual tensor products give squares

**Remember:** The trace of a tensor with its conjugate is an absolute square.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** At an unramified prime p of a unitary cuspidal representation, let A be diagonal with the Satake parameters as entries. The local Rankin–Selberg factor for the representation and its dual is 1/det(I−(A⊗Ā)/pˢ), where Ā denotes complex conjugation.

**Problem.** In −L′(s)/L(s) for this product, the term at pʳ has coefficient (log p)\|tr(Aʳ)\|² for every integer r ≥ 1. Every such coefficient is nonnegative.

**How the definition helps.** The logarithmic derivative gives the coefficient (log p)tr((A⊗Ā)ʳ) in −L′/L (our own derivation). Tensor powers and traces factor, giving (log p)tr(Aʳ)tr(Āʳ) = (log p)\|tr(Aʳ)\|².

**Paper or page:** [Exceptional zeros of Rankin-Selberg L-functions and joint Sato-Tate distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06482v2). It says: “If Π ∈ 𝔄ₙ, then −L′/L(s, Π × Π̃) has non-negative Dirichlet coefficients.”

### Gamma poles delimit the critical integers

**Remember:** A critical integer avoids gamma poles on both sides.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For two full-level holomorphic Hecke cusp forms of even weights k &gt; ℓ, use the normalization reflecting s to k+ℓ−1−s. Call an integer critical when the completing gamma factors are finite there and the dual gamma factors are finite at its reflection.

**Problem.** The critical integers for the Rankin–Selberg function of these two forms are exactly ℓ, ℓ+1, …, k−1.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, checking the definition amounts to imposing one lower bound on each side of reflection. The gamma factors have arguments s and s−ℓ+1, and their poles occur at nonpositive integers. Finiteness therefore requires s ≥ ℓ and k+ℓ−1−s ≥ ℓ. Computing the gamma factors is the separate representation-theoretic step.

**Paper or page:** [An Euler system for the adjoint of a modular form](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04665v2). It says: “The critical values (in the sense of Deligne)”

### Isobaric sums count repeated poles

**Remember:** Each copy pairs with every dual copy of its block.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An isobaric sum Π groups cuspidal representations into a list of blocks, allowing repetitions. Its dual Π̃ replaces each block by its dual. Define L(s,Π×Π̃) by multiplying the Rankin–Selberg factors for all ordered pairs from the two lists. Use unitary blocks whose central characters equal one on positive real scalars.

**Problem.** If each distinct block occurs m times, with m allowed to depend on the block, the pole order at 1 equals ∑ m².

**How the definition helps.** In our own count, the ordered product pairs each copy with every dual copy of the same block. The pole theorem gives a simple pole at 1 precisely for a block paired with its dual. Nonvanishing at 1 for the remaining pairs prevents cancellation.

**Paper or page:** [A new zero-free region for Rankin-Selberg L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16889v6). It says: “If Π is an isobaric sum, then the Rankin–Selberg L-function”

### Pole correction makes convexity uniform

**Remember:** Cancel the pole without changing growth far from it.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take two unitary cuspidal representations π and π′ over a number field, normalized so their central characters equal one on positive real scalars. Write L(s) for their Rankin–Selberg function, formed by pairing their local parameters. Set R(s) = L(s) unless π′ is dual to π. In that case set R(s) = L(s)(s−1)/(s+1).

**Problem.** R is holomorphic for Re s &gt; −1. For σ ≥ 0 and integers j ≥ 0, its jth derivative at σ+it is O(C(t) raised to max(1−σ,0)/2+ε). Here C(t) combines finite and gamma factors at height t, with the constant depending only on ranks, field degree, j and ε &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** The correction cancels the possible pole at 1 and stays bounded on the right half-plane. This gives one estimate even for dual pairs near the pole. In our own explanation, the simple-pole theorem justifies cancellation, strip estimates control size, and Cauchy’s formula bounds derivatives.

**Paper or page:** [Oscillations and first-ever negative Fourier coefficients of symmetric square L-functions over sparse set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18994v1), [A new zero-free region for Rankin-Selberg L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16889v6). It says: “consider the holomorphic function”

### Smooth additive twists have dual length

**Remember:** A smooth twist at length X returns at length q²/X.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let λ(n) denote the normalized Fourier coefficients of a level-one holomorphic Hecke cusp form of weight k. Choose a smooth function v supported in \[1,2\]. Define H(u) = ∫v(y)Jₖ₋₁(4π√(uy))dy over positive y, where Jₖ₋₁ is the Bessel function of the first kind. Put e(x) = exp(2πix).

**Problem.** For coprime integers a,q with q &gt; 0 and X &gt; 0, consider S = ∑ λ(n)e(an/q)v(n/X). If ab ≡ 1 modulo q, then S = (2πiᵏX/q)∑ λ(n)e(−bn/q)H(nX/q²). For fixed k and v, H(u) decays faster than every inverse power as u grows.

**How the definition helps.** Voronoi summation replaces the original smooth weight by its Bessel transform. Substituting y = x/X in that integral gives the prefactor X and argument nX/q² (our own calculation). Repeated integration by parts gives rapid decay because the smooth compactly supported weight contributes no boundary terms.

**Paper or page:** [Subconvexity for GL(1) twists of Rankin-Selberg L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09646v5). It says: “v be a compactly supported smooth function on (0,∞).”

### Monodromy distinguishes Steinberg

**Remember:** The Weil action can agree while monodromy differs.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F70 (Representation-theoretic methods; automorphic representations over local and global fields), 11F85. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a p-adic field K, a two-dimensional Weil–Deligne parameter consists of a complex Weil representation r with open inertia kernel and a nilpotent endomorphism N. They satisfy r(w)Nr(w)⁻¹ = \|w\|N for every Weil element w, where \|w\| is the Weil norm.

**Problem.** The trivial representation and the Steinberg representation have the same Weil action after decomposition into simple factors. Here Steinberg means locally constant complex functions on the projective line modulo constants. Their full parameters differ.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping the operator separates two representations that otherwise have the same data (our own). The operator is zero for the trivial representation and has rank one for Steinberg (our own). The work lies in the local Langlands calculation of these two parameters (our own).

**nLab:** [local Langlands conjecture](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/local+Langlands+conjecture). It says: “A Weil-Deligne representation is a pair (ρ₀,N)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Noninvariant characters induce cusp forms

**Remember:** A character must move under conjugation to give a cusp form.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F70 (Representation-theoretic methods; automorphic representations over local and global fields), 11F41. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a quadratic extension L of a number field F, a Hecke character is a continuous character of the idele class group of L. This group combines local multiplicative groups and identifies tuples differing by a global scalar. Call a character regular if the nonidentity automorphism of L over F changes it.

**Problem.** Automorphic induction transfers the character to a representation of GL₂ over F. This representation is cuspidal, meaning its constant terms vanish, exactly when the character is regular.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity removes exactly the characters whose induction splits as a sum of two characters (our own). For example, the trivial character induces the sum formed from the trivial character and the quadratic character attached to L over F (our own). The quadratic automorphic induction theorem proves the cuspidality criterion.

**Paper or page:** [Vignéras orbifolds: isospectrality, regulators, and torsion homology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07240v1). It says: “is cuspidal if and only if Ψ<sup>σ</sup> ≠ Ψ.”

### Crystalline periods detect good reduction

**Remember:** At the residue prime, test for a full set of crystalline periods.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11G07. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let K be a finite extension of ℚₚ. A p-adic representation describes a continuous Galois action on a finite-dimensional ℚₚ-vector space. Call it crystalline if it has a Galois-fixed basis after extending scalars to Fontaine’s crystalline period ring. This ring supplies coefficients with their own Galois action.

**Problem.** An elliptic curve over K has good reduction if it has a smooth elliptic model over the integers of K. This happens exactly when its rational Tate module, formed from compatible points of p-power order by extending scalars to ℚₚ, is crystalline.

**How the definition helps.** The crystalline test allows the ramification that good elliptic curves can have at p (our own). The curve y² = x³ − x stays smooth modulo five (our own). Its determinant records the action on roots of unity of five-power order, which requires ramified extensions of ℚ₅ (our own). The crystalline comparison theorem proves necessity, and Coleman and Iovita prove sufficiency (our own).

**nLab:** [p-adic Hodge theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/p-adic+Hodge+theory). It says: “We can also apply this construction with Bcrys instead of BdR; if the dimension stays the same we say that V is crystalline.”

**Sources:**

- [Coleman and Iovita, The Frobenius and monodromy operators for curves and abelian varieties](https://doi.org/10.1215/s0012-7094-99-09708-9)

### Determinants retain small-characteristic information

**Remember:** A trace keeps one coefficient, while a determinant law keeps them all.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a commutative ring A and group G, a dimension-d determinant assigns each commutative A-algebra B a unital multiplicative map D<sub>B</sub> from B\[G\] to B. These maps commute with scalar change and satisfy D<sub>B</sub>(bx) = bᵈD<sub>B</sub>(x) for all b ∈ B and x ∈ B\[G\]. Its trace at x is the coefficient of t in D over A\[t\] evaluated at 1+tx.

**Problem.** Over a commutative coefficient ring where d! is invertible, taking traces gives a bijection between dimension-d determinants and trace pseudocharacters. In small characteristic the trace can lose information.

**How the definition helps.** The determinant retains coefficients lost by the trace (our own example). In characteristic two, two copies of any character χ of a cyclic cubic group have trace zero. A nontrivial χ valued in 𝔽₄ has χ² ≠ 1, so its doubled representation has a different determinant from two trivial copies. The cited reconstruction theorem gives the bijection when d! is invertible.

**Paper or page:** [On the relation between pseudocharacters and Chenevier's determinants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18034v1). It says: “a bijection between A-valued d-dimensional determinants on R and A-valued d-dimensional pseudocharacters on R.”

**Sources:**

- [On the relation between pseudocharacters and Chenevier's determinants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18034v1)

### Fontaine's (φ,Γ)-modules are Laurent F-crystals evaluated on one prism

**Remember:** Γ is the symmetry group of one prism, not extra data.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30, 11S20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let K be a finite extension of ℚₚ with integer ring 𝒪 and cyclotomic Galois group Γ = Gal(K(μₚ∞)/K). A Laurent F-crystal assigns each prism (A,I) over 𝒪 a finite projective module over p-completed A\[1/I\], compatibly with base change. Each module carries a compatible isomorphism from its Frobenius pullback.

**Problem.** (φ,Γ)-modules over 𝐀(K) are equivalent to Laurent F-crystals over 𝒪. Wu also shows that Laurent F-crystals are equivalent to ℤₚ-representations of Gal(K̄/K), which gives a new proof of Fontaine's theorem.

**How the definition helps.** Evaluation on Wu’s cyclotomic prism gives a module over 𝐀(K) with invertible linearized Frobenius. Prism automorphisms induce the commuting continuous semilinear Γ-action (our own explanation). Wu’s descent theorem reconstructs the crystal from this (φ,Γ)-module.

It says: “Then (φ,Γ)-modules over 𝐀<sub>K</sub> are equivalent to prismatic F-crystals in 𝒪\_Δ\[1/I\]<sup>∧<sub>p</sub>-modules</sup> over (𝒪<sub>K</sub>)\_Δ.”

### Frames make Galois lifts glue

**Remember:** Fixed matrices glue entry by entry.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a continuous representation ρ̄ of a profinite group G on kⁿ, with k finite of characteristic p. For a complete Noetherian local Witt-vector algebra A with residue field k, a framed lift is a continuous homomorphism G → GLₙ(A) reducing to ρ̄. Equality means equality of the matrices in the fixed basis.

**Problem.** Suppose every open subgroup of G has only finitely many continuous homomorphisms to the group of order p. Then one universal ring parametrizes the framed lifts to all complete Noetherian local algebras over the Witt vectors of k with residue field k.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping the basis lets two compatible lifts glue entry by entry (our own). The resulting matrices still satisfy the group law (our own). Without a frame, gluing also requires a choice of compatible basis changes (our own). Schlessinger’s criterion converts gluing and a finite number of first-order parameters into a universal ring (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Deformation Theory of Galois Representations and the Taylor--Wiles Method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12202v1). It says: “We call the representing ring of it the universal lifting ring or universal framed deformation ring”

### Isogeny degrees determine pairing type

**Remember:** Rescale both pairing inputs, so the multiplier changes by a square.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11G05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For elliptic curves E,F over a number field and an odd prime p, let e<sub>E</sub>,e<sub>F</sub> be their Weil pairings on p-torsion. A linear isomorphism u from E\[p\] to F\[p\] has symplectic type if some a ∈ 𝔽ₚˣ satisfies e<sub>F</sub>(auP,auQ)=e<sub>E</sub>(P,Q) for all P,Q ∈ E\[p\].

**Problem.** An isogeny is a surjective homomorphism of elliptic curves with finite kernel. An isogeny of degree n prime to p induces a torsion isomorphism of symplectic type exactly when n is a square modulo p.

**How the definition helps.** Allowing rescaling turns exact preservation into a square test on the multiplier (our own). Multiplying the map by a scalar multiplies its exponent by that scalar squared (our own). Compatibility of the Weil pairing with the dual isogeny gives the multiplier n (our own). This compatibility supplies the geometric input (our own).

### Kummer-tower (φ,τ)-modules are descent data on the Breuil–Kisin prism

**Remember:** The awkward τ-action is just gluing data over the self-product prism.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30, 11S20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix the Breuil–Kisin prism (𝔖,E) of 𝒪 and its prismatic self-product A⁽²⁾, where 𝒪 is a p-adic integer ring. For an étale φ-module over p-completed 𝔖\[1/E\], a descent datum is a Frobenius-compatible isomorphism between its two pullbacks to p-completed A⁽²⁾\[1/E\]. On the triple product, the isomorphism from the first pullback to the third must equal the composite through the second.

**Problem.** Étale φ-modules over the completed 𝔖\[1/E\] with descent data over the completed A⁽²⁾\[1/E\] are equivalent to étale (φ,τ)-modules. A descent datum is determined by its value at τ.

**How the definition helps.** A descent datum over the self-product is the gluing data that every crystal has, so the ad hoc τ-action becomes standard descent. The comparison with Galois representations then follows from the Laurent F-crystal theorem (our own). The work went into computing A⁽²⁾ and its perfection, and into showing that the value at τ fixes the datum.

### Lifts modulo strict conjugation make the deformation tangent space first Galois cohomology

**Remember:** The group law gives cocycles, and changes of basis give coboundaries.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14D15. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a continuous representation ρ̄ of a profinite group G over a finite field k. A first-order deformation is a continuous lift to k\[ε\]/(ε²), modulo conjugation by matrices reducing to the identity.

**Problem.** The tangent space of the deformation functor of ρ̄ is H¹(G, ad ρ̄). Here ad ρ̄ is the matrix algebra over k, with G acting by conjugation through ρ̄.

**How the definition helps.** The definition makes the tangent space a quotient of cocycles by coboundaries, which is H¹ by definition. A lift g ↦ (1 + εc(g))ρ̄(g) is a homomorphism exactly when c(gh) = c(g) + g·c(h), the cocycle rule (our own). Conjugating by 1 + εX changes c by a coboundary (our own). To read this as the tangent space of a ring needs Mazur's representability theorem, under its hypotheses (our own).

**nLab:** [Galois deformation ring](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Galois+deformation+ring). It says: “where two lifts are considered equivalent if they are conjugate by an element of the kernel of the reduction map.”

**Sources:**

- [Barry Mazur, Deforming Galois representations, in Galois Groups over ℚ (1989)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4613-9649-9_7)

### Log prisms extend the crystalline correspondence to semistable lattices

**Remember:** Add a log structure, and crystalline becomes semistable.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Give the integers 𝒪 of a p-adic field K the log structure from its closed point. A height-h log prismatic F-crystal assigns each log prism (A,I) a finite projective A-module M compatibly with base change. Its compatible linearized Frobenius φ\*M → M is injective with cokernel killed by Iʰ.

**Problem.** On the log prismatic site of 𝒪, F-crystals of height h are equivalent to semistable lattices with Hodge–Tate weights in \[0, h\]. Hodge–Tate weights are integers attached to a representation by its decomposition over the completed algebraic closure. Semistable representations include the Tate modules of curves with semistable reduction (our own gloss).

**How the definition helps.** The log structure is the only change, and it moves the theorem from crystalline to semistable lattices. This matches the move from good reduction to semistable reduction (our own). Without the log structure, the same statement holds with crystalline lattices. The work went into Du and Liu's extension of their (φ,Ĝ)-module construction to log prisms.

**Paper or page:** [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240), [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240). It says: “The category of prismatic F-crystals over (X,M<sub>X</sub>)\_Δ<sub>log</sub> of height h is equivalent to the category of lattices in semi-stable representations of G<sub>K</sub> with Hodge-Tate weights between 0 and h.”

### Oddness excludes nonmodular real representations

**Remember:** Complex conjugation must have opposite signs in the two directions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The absolute Galois group of ℚ consists of the automorphisms of its algebraic closure fixing ℚ. A two-dimensional representation of this group is odd if complex conjugation has determinant −1. In odd characteristic its eigenvalues are then 1 and −1.

**Problem.** Take a continuous odd representation over a finite field of odd characteristic that stays irreducible over the algebraic closure. Serre’s modularity theorem says it arises from a cuspidal modular eigenform, a modular form vanishing at the cusps and diagonalizing the Hecke operators.

**How the definition helps.** Oddness excludes totally real examples with trivial complex conjugation (our own argument). The irreducible cubic x³−4x+1 has positive nonsquare discriminant 229, hence a totally real S₃ splitting field. Its permutation action on the coordinate-sum-zero plane over 𝔽₅ is absolutely irreducible but even. Serre’s modularity theorem supplies modularity under the stated oddness and irreducibility hypotheses.

**Wikipedia:** [Serre's modularity conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre%27s_modularity_conjecture). It says: “Additionally, assume ρ is odd, meaning the image of complex conjugation has determinant -1.”

**Sources:**

- [Khare and Wintenberger, Serre’s modularity conjecture (II)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-009-0206-6)

### Prismatic F-crystals over a p-adic integer ring are crystalline Galois lattices

**Remember:** Crystalline lattices are F-crystals on all prisms at once, with no choices.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30, 11S20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let 𝒪 be the integer ring of a p-adic field K. A prismatic F-crystal assigns each prism (A,I) over 𝒪 a finite projective A-module M compatibly with base change. It carries compatible isomorphisms from φ\*M to M after inverting I, where φ is the prism’s Frobenius.

**Problem.** Prismatic F-crystals over 𝒪 are equivalent to Galois-stable ℤₚ-lattices in crystalline representations of Gal(K̄/K).

**How the definition helps.** The F-crystal uses every prism and no chosen uniformizer, so it describes crystalline lattices integrally and canonically. Kisin's earlier Breuil–Kisin module depends on a uniformizer and its Eisenstein polynomial. Du and Liu's Theorem 4.1.10 says that this module is the value of the crystal at one prism, the Breuil–Kisin prism. The work went into the proof of Bhatt and Scholze, and Du and Liu give a second proof.

**Paper or page:** [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240), [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240). It says: “There is an equivalence of the category of prismatic F-crystals in finite locally free 𝒪\_Δ-modules over (𝒪<sub>K</sub>)\_Δ and the category of Galois stable lattices in crystalline representations of G<sub>K</sub>.”

### Rational Hodge–Tate crystals compute Galois cohomology of nearly Hodge–Tate representations

**Remember:** Reduce modulo the prism ideal, invert p, and require base change.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30, 11S25. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let K be a p-adic field with integer ring 𝒪, completed algebraic closure C and Galois group G = Gal(K̄/K). A rational Hodge–Tate crystal assigns each prism (A,I) over 𝒪 a finite projective (A/I)\[1/p\]-module compatibly with base change. Nearly Hodge–Tate means every Sen weight belongs to ℤ+E′(π)⁻¹𝔪<sub>C</sub>, with π a uniformizer, E its Eisenstein polynomial and 𝔪<sub>C</sub> the maximal ideal of 𝒪<sub>C</sub>.

**Problem.** Evaluation at Fontaine's perfect prism for C, Witt vectors of the tilt of 𝒪(C), gives an equivalence. It goes from rational Hodge–Tate crystals over 𝒪 to nearly Hodge–Tate C-representations, and matches prismatic cohomology with continuous Galois cohomology.

**How the definition helps.** The crystal's one operator plays the role of the Sen operator (our own reading), so Sen theory gets a canonical home on the prismatic site. Sen's classification by linear operators assumes an algebraically closed residue field and is not canonical, as Theorem 8.6 recalls. The work went into Sen theory over the Kummer tower, through locally analytic vectors (Theorem 7.12).

It says: “There exists a natural quasi-isomorphism RΓ((𝒪<sub>K</sub>)\_Δ,\*, 𝕄) ≃ RΓ(G<sub>K</sub>, W) where the right hand side is Galois cohomology.”

### Reducibility ideals locate split traces

**Remember:** One ideal detects every quotient with a split trace.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let T be a two-dimensional Galois pseudocharacter over a complete local ring with 2 invertible and residual trace χ₁+χ₂ for distinct characters. Its reducibility ideal is the least ideal J for which T modulo J is a sum of characters lifting χ₁ and χ₂.

**Problem.** In the cited family of Galois traces attached to modular forms, the reducibility ideal equals the maximal ideal. Among nonzero quotient rings, only the residue field gives a split trace.

**How the definition helps.** The smallest ideal turns a search for two characters into an inclusion test on ideals (our own). A quotient gives a split trace exactly when its defining ideal contains the reducibility ideal (our own). The hard step is the cited calculation of that ideal.

### Requiring an étale Frobenius makes φ-modules match Galois representations

**Remember:** Invertible linearized Frobenius excludes multiplication by p.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11S20, 14F30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let K be a finite extension of ℚₚ, K∞ the field K with all p-power roots of unity, and 𝐀(K) Fontaine's ring for K. An étale φ-module over 𝐀(K) is a finite free module M with a Frobenius-semilinear map whose linearization is an isomorphism. Without the word étale one allows, for example, M = 𝐀(K) with Frobenius x ↦ p·φ(x).

**Problem.** Let 𝐀 be Fontaine's larger completed ring. Taking Frobenius-fixed vectors in M ⊗ 𝐀 is an equivalence from étale φ-modules over 𝐀(K) to ℤₚ-representations of Gal(K̄/K∞).

**How the definition helps.** Fontaine’s equivalence identifies the scalar extension of an étale module with that of its fixed lattice (our own explanation). For the excluded map x ↦ pφ(x), any fixed vector lies in pⁿ𝐀 for every n and hence vanishes. This loses rank one. The quoted Lubin–Tate theorem specializes to the cyclotomic case with coefficient field ℚₚ.

**Paper or page:** [Prismatic F-crystals and Lubin-Tate (φq,Γ)-modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07620). It says: “The functors Mod\_𝐀<sub>K</sub><sup>φ<sub>q</sub>,et</sup> → Rep\_𝒪<sub>L</sub>(G<sub>K∞</sub>), M ↦ (M⊗\_𝐀<sub>K</sub> 𝐀)<sup>φ = 1</sup>, (T⊗\_𝒪<sub>L</sub> 𝐀)<sup>G<sub>K∞</sub></sup> ↤ T form an equivalence of exact tensor categories.”

### The self-product prism gives a one-line criterion for crystalline lattices

**Remember:** Crystalline means τ stays inside the self-product prism.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a p-adic integer ring 𝒪 with residue field k, choose a uniformizer π with Eisenstein polynomial E. Set A = W(k)\[\[u\]\] with φ(u)=uᵖ, and let A⁽²⁾ be the prismatic self-product of (A,(E)) over 𝒪. Thus two maps from this prism into a common prism over 𝒪 induce a unique map from the self-product ring (our own description).

**Problem.** Liu’s (φ,Ĝ)-modules classify lattices in semistable representations with bounded Hodge–Tate weights. Choose the Kummer generator τ acting on compatible roots of π and fixing p-power roots of unity. The associated lattice is crystalline exactly when its underlying Kisin module 𝔐 satisfies τ(𝔐) ⊆ A⁽²⁾ ⊗<sub>A</sub> 𝔐.

**How the definition helps.** Crystalline lattices come from F-crystals on all prisms, and A⁽²⁾ is where such crystals glue, so crystallinity becomes a ring condition on τ. Semistable lattices need a larger ring built from A⁽²⁾ (our own reading). The work went into Du and Liu's prismatic construction of (φ,Ĝ)-modules.

**Paper or page:** [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240). It says: “Select τ ∈ Ĝ as the above. Then T̂(𝔐̂) is crystalline if and only if τ(𝔐) ⊂ A<sup>(2)</sup>⊗<sub>A</sub> 𝔐.”

### Alternation forces a square order

**Remember:** A perfect alternating pairing puts the finite group into pairs.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11G40. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A bilinear pairing b on an abelian group A with values in ℚ/ℤ is alternating if b(x,x) = 0 for every x ∈ A.

**Problem.** If the Tate–Shafarevich group of an elliptic curve over a number field is finite, its order is a square.

**How the definition helps.** Alternation rules out an unpaired cyclic factor of order two (our own). Skew symmetry alone allows the generator of a group of order two to pair with itself to ½ modulo ℤ (our own). For elliptic curves, Cassels proves alternation, and duality makes the pairing perfect when the group is finite (our own). A finite group with a perfect alternating pairing splits into pairs of cyclic factors of equal order, so its order is a square (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Tate–Shafarevich group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate%E2%80%93Shafarevich_group). It says: “if the order of Ш is finite then it is a square.”

### Relaxed Selmer conditions pair with strict ones

**Remember:** Opposite local conditions make the two dimension jumps add to half the local dimension.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11R34. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix an elliptic curve over a number field and a prime p. Its p-Selmer group consists of global Galois cohomology classes on the points killed by p that locally come from dividing curve points by p. At one finite prime, the relaxed group allows every local class and the strict group requires zero. Both keep the usual conditions elsewhere.

**Problem.** The relaxed dimension minus the strict dimension equals half the dimension of local first cohomology at the chosen prime. All dimensions use the field of p elements.

**How the definition helps.** Allowing everything and allowing zero give opposite local conditions under the local duality pairing (our own). The usual condition pairs to zero with itself and has half the local dimension (our own). The two global dimension jumps give images in the usual local condition and its dual (our own). The cited orthogonality theorem makes these images exact annihilators, so their dimensions add to the dimension of the usual condition (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Increasing the p-Selmer rank by twisting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09207v3). It says: “The images of the two right-hand maps in the following exact sequences are orthogonal complements of each other under the sum of the local Tate pairings.”

### Exterior powers give determinant characters

**Remember:** Take the top exterior power before passing to the Galois action.

**Problem.** At a prime different from the characteristic, the Galois action on the determinant module’s Tate module equals the determinant of the original Galois action. The Tate module records compatible points killed by powers of that prime.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, a linear transformation acts on the top exterior power by its determinant. The cited theorem realizes the resulting motive by a unique rank-one Drinfeld module up to isomorphism. Applying the linear calculation to torsion also requires the comparison between motives and Tate modules to preserve exterior powers.

### Frobenius polynomials classify Drinfeld isogeny classes

**Remember:** The Frobenius polynomial determines the isogeny class over a finite field.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix A = 𝔽q\[T\]. A Drinfeld module lets A act by additive polynomials, and its characteristic ideal is the kernel of the scalar map to the base field. At a different prime, collect compatible points killed by powers of that prime and invert the prime to form the rational Tate module. Define the Frobenius polynomial as the characteristic polynomial of the field-size power map on this space.

**Problem.** Take two Drinfeld modules of the same rank and characteristic over the same finite field. Their Frobenius polynomials agree exactly when an isogeny, a nonzero map respecting both actions, exists over that field.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, one polynomial lets us state the classification as equality of two computable invariants. An isogeny identifies the rational Tate modules and carries one Frobenius action to the other. Conversely, Frobenius acts semisimply, so its polynomial determines the rational representation. The Tate isogeny theorem turns this linear comparison into an isogeny.

### Ideal classes classify rank one Drinfeld modules

**Remember:** At rank one, period lattices become fractional ideals up to scaling.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.), 11R58. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Problem.** The ideal class group acts freely and transitively on the rank one Drinfeld modules up to isomorphism.

**How the definition helps.** A basis for the lattice’s span over the fraction field identifies the lattice with a fractional ideal of A (our own argument). **Remember:** An edge length is a valuation, so ramification multiplies it.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G20 (Curves over finite and local fields), 14G20. arXiv math.AG, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A split semistable curve model has a reduced special fiber whose only singularities are crossings with two branches over the residue field. Draw a vertex for each component and an edge for each crossing. In completed local coordinates, write a crossing as xy = a. Give its edge length v(a), where the valuation v counts powers of a generator of the maximal ideal.

**Problem.** Start with such a model over a complete discrete valuation ring. After a finite totally ramified extension of index e, the pulled-back model has the same graph with every length multiplied by e.

**How the definition helps.** The pulled-back node still has equation xy = a, so its length is the new normalized valuation of a (our own calculation). This valuation restricts to e times the old one. Total ramification preserves the residue field, hence the special fibre and its graph.

**Paper or page:** [Models of Bihyperelliptic Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09730v1). It says: “with the same dual graph as 𝒞, but with the lengths of all edges multiplied by e.”

### Under semistability, invariant valuations determine the reduction graph of hyperelliptic curves

**Remember:** Require semistability before reading a reduction graph from invariants.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G20 (Curves over finite and local fields), 14H45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A hyperelliptic curve has a degree-two map to the projective line. It is semistable if it has a proper flat model over the ring of integers whose special fibre is reduced, with only ordinary double points. The dual graph of the special fibre has a vertex for each component and an edge for each double point.

**Problem.** Let C be a hyperelliptic curve of genus g ≥ 2 over a local field K of odd residue characteristic. The paper gives a finite list of invariants that depends only on g. If C is semistable, their valuations determine the dual graph of its minimal regular model over the maximal unramified extension of K.

**How the definition helps.** Semistability removes the curves whose graph the invariants cannot see, so the valuations then determine the graph. The paper shows by a counterexample that, for genus at least two, no list of invariants works for curves that are not semistable. The result is the analog of Tate’s algorithm, where ord(j) gives the graph of a semistable elliptic curve. The work is the explicit method that reads the graph from the valuations.

**Paper or page:** [Invariants recovering the reduction type of a hyperelliptic curve](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08487v3). It says: “They also determine the dual graph of the special fibre of the minimal regular model of C/Kᵘⁿʳ if C/K is semistable.”

### Serre–Frobenius groups separate ordinary and supersingular curves

**Remember:** Close the powers of the normalized Frobenius tuple inside a torus.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G25 (Varieties over finite and local fields), 11G10, 11G20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an abelian variety over 𝔽q, let u be the tuple of complex Frobenius eigenvalues divided by √q. Its Serre–Frobenius group is the closure of {uⁿ : n ∈ ℤ} in the product of unit circles.

**Problem.** Normalized Frobenius traces are equidistributed for the image of Haar probability measure under the coordinate sum. For elliptic curves the group is a circle exactly in the ordinary case. The supersingular case gives exactly the cyclic orders 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12.

**How the definition helps.** Powers of a topological generator equidistribute for Haar measure, and summing coordinates gives the traces (our own explanation). For elliptic curves the two coordinates are inverses, so one determines the group. The classification of elliptic Frobenius eigenvalues gives the listed root-of-unity orders in the supersingular case and an infinite, hence dense, circle subgroup otherwise.

**Paper or page:** [Frobenius distributions of low dimensional abelian varieties over finite fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02237), [Frobenius distributions of low dimensional abelian varieties over finite fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02237). ### Regular dessins descend to moduli fields

**Remember:** A regular cover can move any chosen sheet to any other.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G32 (Arithmetic aspects of dessins d'enfants, Bely? theory), 14H57. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A dessin is a connected cover of the sphere branched only over 0, 1 and ∞. Call it regular if its symmetries over the sphere act transitively on each unbranched fiber. Its field of moduli consists of the algebraic numbers fixed by every Galois automorphism preserving its isomorphism class.

**Problem.** Every regular dessin admits defining equations over its field of moduli.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity makes the deck group act simply transitively above the rational unbranched value 2 (our own argument). Mark a point there and use the unique deck transformation adjusting each conjugate isomorphism to preserve the marking. Uniqueness gives the cocycle condition, so Weil descent gives equations over the field of moduli.

**Remember:** The modulus D bounds ramification along the boundary, as a conductor does.

**Definition.** For a proper variety X and effective Cartier divisor D, start with the free abelian group on closed points outside D. Quotient by pushed-forward principal divisors from normalizations of integral curves in X meeting the complement. Use rational functions congruent to one modulo the pulled-back divisor, retaining its multiplicities.

Assume the boundary supports an effective Cartier divisor, and let D range over effective Cartier divisors with that support. **How the definition helps.** Increasing the multiplicities allows increasing ramification along the same boundary (our own explanation). The reciprocity theorem identifies the resulting finite quotients in the inverse limit, using Bloch’s formula with modulus.
