### Invariant metrics scale heights exactly

**Remember:** An invariant metric turns pullback into exact multiplication of heights.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G50 (Heights), 14G40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f be an endomorphism of a projective variety over a number field. Fix an ample line bundle L and an isomorphism from f\*L to its qth tensor power for some integer q &gt; 1. A continuous adelic metric on L is invariant if this isomorphism preserves the metrics at every place.

**Problem.** For such a map, invariant norms exist, and the height h that they define satisfies h(f(P)) = qh(P).

**How the definition helps.** The invariant norms make pullback multiply the height exactly, in our own explanation. Arbitrary norms on the same bundle generally give this relation only up to bounded error. Heights pull back with maps and add when bundles are tensored. The existence theorem constructs the compatible norms by repeated pullback and normalization, starting with norms from an integral model outside finitely many places.

### Alternating Kummer products give symmetric powers

**Remember:** Alternating the relative product makes the Kummer tensors symmetric.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Work over the rational affine line with 0 and 1 removed, using coordinate z. The Kummer motive K records degree-one cohomology of the multiplicative line relative to the points 1 and 1/z. Take degree-n relative cohomology of its n-fold product, marking every face where a coordinate equals either point. Select the part where exchanging two coordinates acts by minus one.

**Problem.** This part of the relative cohomology motive is the symmetric tensor power Symⁿ(K).

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, selecting the sign cancels the sign already contributed by exchanging two degree-one cohomology factors. The relative product theorem identifies the whole group with a tensor power and explains this extra sign. The selected part therefore corresponds to symmetric tensors. This realizes the abstract symmetric power by an explicit product of marked lines.

### Clean polylogarithms erase product terms

**Remember:** Project away products before taking a single-valued period.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Represent a multiple polylogarithm by its formal iterated integral, with weight equal to the number of integrations. Take its de Rham image, which retains its algebraic differential data. Apply the Dynkin projection, a linear operator whose kernel in positive weight consists of sums of products of positive-weight elements. Evaluate the single-valued period and take its real part in odd weight or its imaginary part in even weight.

**Problem.** Suppose a rational linear combination of formal integrals of the same positive weight equals a sum of products of positive-weight elements. The corresponding clean functions then sum to zero with the same coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** The projection kills the entire sum before numerical evaluation. Our own comparison is with ordinary single-valued evaluation, which preserves multiplication and can retain nonzero products. The substantive step identifies the kernel of the Dynkin projection.

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344), [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344). It says: “The kernel of Π is generated by all non-trivial products”

### Clean polylogarithms reverse interior letters

**Remember:** After products vanish, reversal preserves odd lengths and negates even lengths.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a formal iterated integral with fixed endpoints, apply the Dynkin projection to its de Rham image and evaluate its single-valued period. The clean value takes the real part in odd length and the imaginary part in even length.

**Problem.** In a clean iterated integral of length n &gt; 0, reversing the interior letters multiplies it by (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ without exchanging endpoints.

**How the definition helps.** The shuffle antipode identity expresses the word plus (−1)ⁿ times its reversal as a sum of products from nonempty proper cuts (our own explanation). The Dynkin projection kills those products. Evaluating the remaining two terms gives the claimed sign with unchanged endpoints.

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344). It says: “Iᶜˢᵛ(x₀; xₙ, …, x₁; xₙ₊₁) = (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ Iᶜˢᵛ(x₀; x₁, …, xₙ; xₙ₊₁).”

### Clean projection gives tetralogarithm reduction

**Remember:** Remove all products, then fix the constant on real inputs.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 33B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write I₃,₁(x,y) for the nested integral from 0 to 1 with successive poles x,0,0,y, using the paper’s clean evaluation. This evaluation first projects formal integrals of weight four along products of integrals of smaller weight. It then takes the imaginary part of their single-valued evaluation. Write L₄ for the same evaluation of the fourth polylogarithm.

**Problem.** For x,y∉{0,1}, with y∉{x,1−x} and all displayed arguments of L₄ outside {0,1}, I₃,₁(1−x,y)+I₃,₁(x,y)=L₄((1−x)/(1−y))−L₄((1−y)/x)−3L₄(y/(1−x))−3L₄(y/x)+L₄(y/(y−1))−L₄((1−x)y/(x(1−y)))/2−L₄(xy/((1−x)(1−y)))/2+L₄((1−y)y/((1−x)x))/2.

**How the definition helps.** The clean projection removes the lower-weight products and taking the imaginary part fixes the constant on real inputs. The work goes into Gangl’s matching of the symbols, which record the successive logarithmic differentials, modulo products.

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344v2). It says: “This constant must be 0 since each side vanishes on the real line, as we take the imaginary part in the definition of the functions.”

### Cobrackets rule out classical tetralogarithms

**Remember:** A nonzero two-by-two split rules out a classical expression.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Give each polylogarithm symbol a weight equal to its tensor length. Quotient positive-weight symbols by sums of products of positive-weight symbols. For a weight-four symbol, split after its second position and subtract the result with the two halves exchanged. Take both halves modulo products to obtain the weight-(2,2) cobracket.

**Problem.** The weight-(2,2) cobracket vanishes on every rational sum of classical tetralogarithm symbols modulo products. Thus a nonzero value rules out any such expression.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, this test selects the split where the classical tetralogarithm has a repeated logarithm in its second half. That two-letter tensor is half the shuffle square of the logarithm, so it vanishes modulo products. Linearity gives the same result for any rational sum. Applying this obstruction to a particular function requires computing its cobracket.

**Paper or page:** [Cluster Polylogarithms I: Quadrangular Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.01564). It says: “For $k\\geq 2$ iterated truncated coproduct $\\overline{\\Delta }<sup>\[k-1\]</sup>$ vanishes on $\\mathcal{D}<sub>k-1</sub>\\mathcal{L}\_\\bullet (\\mathrm{F})$”

**Remember:** Equal divisor differences give equal regulator periods without integrating twice.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19F27. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On an elliptic curve, the divisor of a function lists its zeros and poles with signed multiplicities. The diamond product replaces a pair of points P and Q by their group difference P−Q, multiplying their multiplicities. Add the results and impose \[−P\] = −\[P\].

**Problem.** Take two pairs of rational functions on an elliptic curve E over ℚ, with rational zeros and poles. Assume their symbols extend across every point. Equal diamond products give equal regulator values on a generator of H₁(E,ℤ)⁻, the subgroup where complex conjugation acts by negation.

**How the definition helps.** In our own comparison, the diamond product turns two period calculations into one equality between formal sums of points. Bloch’s formula evaluates each period by applying the same real-valued function, the elliptic dilogarithm, to that sum. The elliptic dilogarithm changes sign under negation, so it respects the imposed relation. The formula supplies the link with integration.

### Five-term relations give a regulator

**Remember:** The five-term identity lets the dilogarithm act on classes of symbols.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a subfield F of ℂ, start with formal integer sums of symbols \[x\], where x belongs to F and differs from 0 and 1. For distinct such x and y impose \[x\]−\[y\]+\[y/x\]−\[(1−x⁻¹)/(1−y⁻¹)\]+\[(1−x)/(1−y)\]=0. The resulting quotient is the pre-Bloch group.

**Problem.** The Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm D gives a homomorphism \[x\] ↦ D(x) from the pre-Bloch group to ℝ.

**How the definition helps.** Our own explanation uses the quotient to replace checking every change of representative with checking one family of relations. The analytic five-term identity says exactly that D sends each defining relation to zero.

### Integrable symbols exclude path dependence

**Remember:** Adjacent wedge tests remove the local obstruction to path independence.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a smooth complex variety, remove the zeros and poles of the rational functions under consideration. Represent each function f by the differential form df/f, and represent ordered lists of these forms by tensors. For each adjacent pair, replace its two forms by their exterior product, leaving the other positions intact. A sum of tensors is integrable when every such replacement gives zero after summing.

**Problem.** An integrable tensor gives a homotopy-invariant linear combination of logarithmic iterated integrals. Homotopies fix both endpoints and stay in the open variety.

**How the definition helps.** Chen’s variation formula has only adjacent wedge terms here, since logarithmic differentials are closed (our own explanation). Integrability makes each such term vanish. For dx/x followed by dy/y, move from (1,1) to (2,2) along coordinate segments. Moving first in x gives (log 2)², while the homotopic path moving first in y gives zero (our own example).

**nLab:** [iterated integral](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/iterated+integral), [polylogarithm](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/polylogarithm). It says: “Iterated integrals include nested integration of differential forms”

**Remember:** The antipode inverts the whole variation matrix.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Arrange the formal coefficients of multiple polylogarithms in their triangular variation matrix V, with ones on the diagonal. Write W for its transpose. The coproduct splits Wᵢⱼ into the sum of Wᵢₖ ⊗ Wₖⱼ over intermediate indices k.

**Problem.** The antipode, the operation undoing a coproduct under multiplication, sends V entry by entry to V⁻¹.

**How the definition helps.** The matrix coproduct turns the antipode axiom into S(W)W = I (our own calculation). Hence S(W) = W⁻¹, and transposition gives S(V) = V⁻¹ since the coefficient algebra is commutative. The substantive input is the coproduct formula for the variation matrix.

### Multiplication identifies torsion logarithm fibers

**Remember:** Multiplication sends torsion to zero and rescales each graded piece invertibly.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let π be the fundamental group of a complex elliptic curve at zero. In its rational group ring, let I be the ideal of sums whose coefficients add to zero. Keep terms through degree n by taking the quotient by Iⁿ⁺¹. The pointed logarithm system transports this vector space along loops by group multiplication and marks the element 1 at zero.

**Problem.** For N ≥ 1, multiplication by N identifies this system with its pullback, whose fiber at P is the original fiber at NP. Thus every point killed by N has a canonical identification of its fiber with the fiber at zero.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplication by N sends each loop γ to γᴺ and hence induces a map on the truncated group ring (our own argument). This map preserves the marked unit and intertwines transport with pullback transport. On degree k of the associated graded ring it acts by Nᵏ, so it is invertible over ℚ. At a point P killed by N the pullback fibre is the fibre at zero.

**Remember:** Two cuts give the same nested lists whichever cut comes first.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Represent an iterated integral by a word listing its integration forms between two endpoints. Define its coproduct, a rule giving pairs of factors, by summing over all subsequences of interior letters. The first factor keeps the selected letters. The second multiplies the integrals between successive selected positions, counting both endpoints as boundaries.

**Problem.** Splitting the first factor again gives the same three-factor sum as splitting the second factor again.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, both expansions list exactly the same pairs of nested subsequences. One expansion chooses the larger subsequence first. The other chooses the smaller subsequence first, then selects additional letters in each gap. The comparison with the coproduct defined by periods still requires the theorem identifying it with the cut formula.

**Remember:** Only boundary-zero dilogarithm symbols represent classes in rational indecomposable K₃.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an infinite field F, form rational sums of symbols \[x\] with x ≠ 0,1. Impose the alternating relation among the five cross-ratios obtained by deleting one of five distinct projective points. This gives the rational pre-Bloch group. Its Bloch subgroup consists of sums with zero boundary under \[x\] ↦ x ∧ (1 − x), using the rational exterior square of F×.

**Problem.** Suslin identifies the rational Bloch group with indecomposable K₃ of F over ℚ. Here indecomposable means taking the quotient by the image of Milnor K₃, the subgroup generated by triple products of units.

**How the definition helps.** The boundary test excludes \[t\] over ℚ(t) (our own example). The orders at zero and one send t and 1−t to independent basis vectors, so their wedge is nonzero. Suslin’s exact sequence maps indecomposable K₃ onto the Bloch group with torsion kernel, giving the asserted rational isomorphism.

**Remember:** Changing the representative only shifts the sum.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 33B30. arXiv math.NT, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix q with 0&lt;\|q\|&lt;1. The complex elliptic curve E identifies nonzero numbers x and qx. Define its elliptic dilogarithm at x by summing the Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm D(qᵏx) over all integers k, using D(1)=0.

**Problem.** The orbit sum is absolutely convergent and gives a well-defined function on E. It also changes sign under x ↦ 1/x.

**How the definition helps.** Our own explanation sums over all representatives because the ordinary dilogarithm D(x) can depend on the choice of x. Multiplying x by q only shifts the summation index. Replacing k by −k and using D(1/z)=−D(z) gives the sign under inversion. Absolute convergence follows from D(z)=O(\|z\|(1+\|log\|z\|\|)) near zero and inversion for the other tail.

### Orbit sums give elliptic doubling

**Remember:** Group even and odd orbit indices after pairing opposite roots.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 14H52. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Represent a complex elliptic curve by nonzero complex numbers modulo multiplication by powers of q, with 0 &lt; \|q\| &lt; 1. Write D for the Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm, Im Li₂(z) + arg(1−z) log\|z\|, extended continuously at 0 and 1. Define Dᴱ(\[z\]) by summing D(qⁿz) over all integers n.

**Problem.** For every P ∈ E, twice the sum of Dᴱ(Q) over the four points with 2Q = P equals Dᴱ(P).

**How the definition helps.** The ordinary doubling formula D(v²)=2(D(v)+D(−v)) pairs opposite roots (our own argument). Choose w² = z, so w, −w, √q w and −√q w represent the four halves. The first pair gives the even orbit indices and the second gives the odd indices. Absolute convergence allows the two sums to be combined.

### Path truncation makes monodromy unipotent

**Remember:** Loop differences become nilpotent when long products vanish.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.AG, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On the projective line punctured at 0, 1 and ∞, use a tangential base point at zero and write J for the rational augmentation ideal. It is generated by γ−1 as γ ranges over based loops up to homotopy. Truncation at degree n means passing to the quotient of the rational group algebra by Jⁿ⁺¹.

**Problem.** Continuing the finite polylogarithm system around any loop gives a unipotent operator M. This means that some power of M − I is zero.

**How the definition helps.** In a degree-n truncation, right multiplication by γ−1 has vanishing (n+1)st power (our own argument). Hain realizes the finite polylogarithm monodromy on a quotient of such a truncation. In the full completion a loop around zero maps to a generator of a cyclic quotient, where its difference from one has no vanishing power.

It says: “It has unipotent monodromy at each point of {0,1,∞}.”

### Projecting products makes relations exact

**Remember:** Project away products before you evaluate the periods.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 33B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Represent a polylogarithm by its formal integral before evaluating it as a function. The number of integrations gives its weight. In the associated de Rham algebra of formal integrals, apply the authors’ projection Π, whose kernel consists of sums of positive-weight products. Evaluate the result as a single-valued function, taking its real part in odd weight and its imaginary part in even weight.

**Problem.** Suppose a rational sum of formal polylogarithms of one weight equals a sum of products of positive weights. Its clean single-valued evaluation is zero.

**How the definition helps.** The projection kills products before the ordinary single-valued evaluation can give them nonzero values. Proposition 2.4 identifies its kernel. Our own explanation then uses linearity to pass from individual products to any sum of products.

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344v2). It says: “The kernel of Π is generated by all non-trivial products”

### Rational Bloch regulators are injective

**Remember:** Rational coefficients remove classes that every real regulator must kill.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F be a number field, a finite extension of ℚ. Form rational sums of symbols \[x\] for x in F other than 0 and 1, subject to the dilogarithm’s five-term relations. The rational Bloch group consists of classes with Σa\[x\] mapping to zero under \[x\] ↦ x ∧ (1−x). Here ∧ denotes the alternating product on the multiplicative group of F with rational coefficients.

**Problem.** Choose one embedding σ from each conjugate pair of nonreal embeddings of F. Evaluating the Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm D gives an injective map with coordinates ΣaD(σ(x)).

**How the definition helps.** Rational coefficients remove elements of finite order, which every homomorphism to a real vector space kills. Our own explanation uses Borel’s regulator theorem to establish injectivity after this step. The comparison with the dilogarithm regulator identifies its coordinates.

**nLab:** [Bloch group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Bloch+group). It says: “Now the point is that restricted to the Bloch group proper the Borel regulator is injective.”

### Regulator forms kill Steinberg relations

**Remember:** The dilogarithm turns the Steinberg relation into an exact differential.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19D45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a smooth complex curve, take rational functions f and g without zeros or poles on an open set U. Set η(f,g) = log\|f\| d arg g − log\|g\| d arg f, where d arg records angular change. A Steinberg symbol {f,g} turns multiplication in either entry into addition and satisfies {f,1−f} = 0 whenever both entries qualify.

**Problem.** Sending {f,g} to the class of η(f,g) gives a well-defined map from Steinberg symbols to closed real 1-forms on U, modulo differentials of single-valued functions.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, passing to classes checks all closed-path integrals at once. Roy proves that η is closed and turns multiplication into addition in each entry. He also identifies η(f,1−f) as the differential of the single-valued Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm D(f). Its class therefore vanishes, exactly as the Steinberg relation requires.

**Paper or page:** [Generalized Mahler measures of Laurent polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04601). It says: “\\eta \\left(x, 1-x\\right) = d D\\left(x\\right).”

### Residues identify elliptic polylogarithms

**Remember:** Once the residue is fixed, there is no class left to add.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a complex elliptic curve, remove the D² points killed by multiplication by an integer D ≥ 2. Use the logarithm system of coefficients, which transports truncated power series in two loop variables along paths. At each removed point the residue measures the local cohomology class around that puncture. Define the elliptic polylogarithm as the compatible sequence of degree-one classes with scalar residue D²−1 at zero and −1 at every other puncture.

**Problem.** There is exactly one compatible sequence of degree-one classes with these residues, so the elliptic polylogarithm is well defined. The residues are read through the splitting at each removed point given by multiplication by D, and they have zero components in all positive degrees.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, defining the class by residues replaces comparison of global representatives by local calculations at finitely many points. Sprang’s exact sequence shows that residues determine the class after taking all truncations together. It also shows that the specified residues occur, since their scalar components sum to zero. Sprang computes these residues for explicit differential forms from the Poincaré line bundle, proving that they represent the polylogarithm.

**nLab:** [Poincaré line bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Poincar%C3%A9+line+bundle). It says: “The canonical line bundle on the product of an abelian group (abelian variety) and its dual Picard scheme.”

### Steinberg symbols yield elliptic identities

**Remember:** One Steinberg relation gives a whole sum of elliptic dilogarithm values.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19D45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a rational function f, its divisor div(f) lists its zeros and poles with signed multiplicities. The diamond product ⋄ replaces each pair of divisor points P,Q by P−Q and multiplies their multiplicities. Add the results, with a point and its negative carrying opposite signs. A Steinberg symbol {f,g} is additive under multiplication in either entry and obeys {f,1−f} = 0.

**Problem.** Take a nonconstant rational function f on an elliptic curve over ℚ. Assume its zeros, its poles and all points where f equals one are rational. Applying the elliptic dilogarithm linearly to div(f) ⋄ div(1−f) gives zero.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the symbol definition replaces a sum of special function values with one defining relation. Bloch’s formula identifies that sum with the regulator of {f,1−f}, a period integral depending additively on the symbol. The defining relation makes the symbol zero, and its period therefore vanishes.

### Three terms compute next-to-Milnor cohomology

**Remember:** Next to Milnor degree, only three terms affect the answer.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19E15. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F be a field of characteristic zero, m ≥ 3, and V = F× ⊗ ℚ. In degree m−1, Goncharov’s complex uses B₂(F) ⊗ Λᵐ⁻²V, where B₂(F) is the rational space of dilogarithm symbols modulo their functional relations. The differential sends \[x\]₂ ⊗ β to (1−x) ∧ x ∧ β.

**Problem.** Quotient the kernel by the span of \[x\]₂ ⊗ (x ∧ α) for x ∈ F outside {0,1} and α ∈ Λᵐ⁻³V. This quotient gives rational motivic cohomology of F in degree m−1 and weight m, also defined using algebraic cycles.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the symbol complex reduces this description to one kernel and one family of boundaries. Each incoming relation is the image of a trilogarithm symbol tensored with α. Computing cohomology here needs only these two arrows. Identifying the answer with the group defined using algebraic cycles requires Bolbachan’s comparison theorem.

### Top polylogarithm cohomology gives Milnor K-theory

**Remember:** The last differential lists exactly the relations of Milnor K-theory.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19D45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an infinite field F, put V = Fˣ ⊗ ℚ and fix m ≥ 2. Goncharov’s last differential maps B₂(F) ⊗ Λᵐ⁻²V to ΛᵐV, where B₂(F) is the rational dilogarithm symbol space modulo five-term relations. It sends each \[x\] ⊗ α to (1 − x) ∧ x ∧ α for x ∈ F outside {0,1}.

**Problem.** For m ≥ 2, the top cohomology of this complex is the rational Milnor K-group of F in degree m.

**How the definition helps.** The displayed images span precisely the Steinberg relations in the exterior-power presentation of rational Milnor K-theory (our own). Top cohomology takes the quotient of ΛᵐV by their span.

### Truncated cuts vanish in lower depth

**Remember:** A surviving cut needs one depth letter in every factor.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A formal iterated integral class has depth at most d if words with at most d nonzero interior letters represent it modulo products and linearity. The truncated cobracket discards all terms of the ordinary cobracket with a weight-one factor.

**Problem.** For k ≥ 2, this k-factor operation vanishes on classes of depth at most k − 1. On depth k its value therefore depends only on the class modulo lower depth.

**How the definition helps.** Every surviving factor needs a nonzero interior letter because depth-zero integrals are powers of logarithms and products vanish (our own). Truncation removes the remaining weight-one logarithms. The cut formula bounds total depth by input depth, so k surviving factors require depth at least k.

**Remember:** The dilogarithm has just one intermediate weight to cut.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Problem.** For z ∈ ℂ outside {0,1}, the reduced coproduct is log(1 − z) ⊗ log z. Each logarithm represents a class modulo 2πiℤ in the integral normalization.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, framing makes the single intermediate basis vector supply the only term. Reading the two adjacent entries in units of their diagonal periods gives log(1 − z) and log z. The scalar dilogarithm alone does not record both entries. Constructing the period matrix and proving basis independence supply the substantive work.

### Weight-one symbols multiply by shuffling

**Remember:** The symbol shuffles the lists of weight-one entries.

**Problem.** The symbol of a product equals the shuffle product of the two symbols.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplicativity of the coproduct makes each weight-one position take weight one from one input and zero from the other (our own). The counit removes the scalar positions. Choosing the positions supplied by the first input gives every shuffle with its multiplicity.

### Fourier signs bound lattice packing

**Remember:** One sign controls the lattice and the other controls its dual.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H31 (Lattice packing and covering (number-theoretic aspects)), 11H60. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix r &gt; 0 and use the Fourier kernel exp(−2πix·ξ) on ℝⁿ. An admissible function is a real radial Schwartz function f with f(x) ≤ 0 whenever ‖x‖ ≥ r. Require f̂(ξ) ≥ 0 for every ξ and f(0) = f̂(0) &gt; 0.

**Problem.** If such a function exists, any lattice packing by balls of radius r/2 has density at most the volume of one such ball. For a unit-covolume lattice with shortest length r, the bound is sharp.

**How the definition helps.** The signs give ∑ᵥ f(v) ≤ f(0) on the packing lattice and ∑ᵤ f̂(u) ≥ f̂(0) on its dual (our own). Poisson summation equates the first sum to the second divided by the lattice covolume. The covolume is therefore at least one, with equality giving the claimed density.

**Problem.** Let d(t) denote the distance to the nearest integer. The lower limit of q·d(qα)·d(qβ) over positive integers q is zero exactly when this orbit has noncompact closure.

**How the definition helps.** The lattice records both approximation errors and their common denominator, and each diagonal map preserves their product (our own). The dynamical correspondence for Littlewood’s conjecture equates lower limit zero with arbitrarily short nonzero vectors in the forward orbit. **Remember:** Shortest vectors fix the form and balance its volume.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H55 (Quadratic forms (reduction theory, extreme forms, etc.)), 11H31. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a positive definite form with matrix Q, let S contain vvᵀ for every nonzero integer vector v minimizing vᵀQv. Voronoi’s theorem proves that together these tests characterize a local density maximum.

Uniform improvement holds exactly when the moving lattice eventually avoids a neighborhood of the critical locus.

They form a torsor, a space on which the comparison symmetries act freely and transitively after extending scalars.

**Problem.** The number of algebraically independent entries of the actual comparison matrix is at most the dimension of the motivic Galois group of the motive.

**How the definition helps.** The torsor presents the period integrals as values of coordinate functions at a single complex point. In our own argument, their transcendence degree cannot exceed the dimension of the space containing that point. ### Quotients bound p-adic period fields

**Remember:** Subtract the symmetry that fixes the embedded classes.

*True by definition.* MSC 11J81 (Transcendence (general theory)), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a pure motive M over ℚ̄ in Ancona and Fratila’s graded category with good reduction at a chosen prime above p. Its period space parametrizes embeddings of specialized algebraic cycle classes into the de Rham cohomology of the corresponding objects before reduction. Require these embeddings to respect all maps and tensor products in the category generated by M.

**Problem.** The transcendence degree of André’s p-adic periods over ℚ̄ is at most dim GdR − dim Gcrys. These groups describe tensor symmetries of de Rham cohomology before reduction and crystalline cohomology after reduction.

**How the definition helps.** The period space makes the numerical periods values of algebraic functions at the comparison point. In our own argument, no point can yield more algebraically independent coordinates than the dimension of its space. The homogeneous-space theorem computes that dimension by subtracting the dimension of the stabilizer Gcrys from that of the acting group GdR.

**Paper or page:** [Algebraic classes in mixed characteristic and André's p-adic periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.09213v2). It says: “trdegℚ̄ 𝒫ₚ(M) ≤ trdegℚ̄ 𝒫ₚ(⟨M⟩) ≤ dim GdR(M) − dim Gcrys(M).”

### Relative periods isolate moving relations

**Remember:** Fix the constant motives before testing relations among moving periods.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J81 (Transcendence (general theory)), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a finitely generated extension k of ℂ and a Zariski-dense real analytic arc on a model of k extending past both endpoints. Relative comparisons are tensor isomorphisms between de Rham and Betti realizations that agree with the usual comparison on every constant object. The relative formal period ring is the coordinate ring of these comparisons.

**Problem.** Evaluation identifies the relative formal period ring with the ring of analytic period germs. A germ records a function only near the chosen arc point.

**How the definition helps.** Fixing the constant comparisons lets injectivity express exactly which relations hold among the varying periods, in our own interpretation. A formal relation holds whenever its evaluation vanishes. Bakker and Tsimerman prove injectivity using their functional transcendence theorem.

**Paper or page:** [Functional Transcendence of Periods and the Geometric André–Grothendieck Period Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05182v2). It says: “The relative period ring ℙ̃(k/ℂ) is an integral domain, and the evaluation map evₖ is an isomorphism.”

### Counting only reduced fractions frees multiplicative Khintchine from monotonicity

**Remember:** Count each rational point once, and monotonicity is no longer needed.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J83 (Metric theory), 11J13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Approximate a vector α in ℝᵏ by fractions p₁/q, …, pₖ/q with one common denominator q. Require every numerator pᵢ to be coprime to q. Measure the error as the product of the k coordinate errors \|αᵢ − pᵢ/q\|.

**Problem.** Let ψ map positive integers to \[0,1/2\]. Almost every α admits infinitely many reduced approximations of product error at most ψ(q)/qᵏ exactly when ∑<sub>q≥1</sub> ψ(q)(φ(q)/q)ᵏ(log(q/(φ(q)ψ(q))))ᵏ⁻¹ diverges. Here φ is Euler’s totient function, and denominators with ψ(q) = 0 contribute zero.

**How the definition helps.** Coprimality counts distinct rational coordinates and leaves φ(q) residue classes per coordinate (our own). This gives the totient weight in the multiplicative Duffin–Schaeffer theorem. Its overlap estimates establish divergence without assuming monotonicity.

**Paper or page:** [The Duffin-Schaeffer Conjecture for multiplicative Diophantine approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11257v1). It says: “The recent result of Koukoulopoulos and Maynard provides an elegant way of removing monotonicity when only counting reduced fractions.”

**Sources:**

### Reduced fractions remove monotonicity from Khintchine's theorem

**Remember:** Count each fraction once, in lowest terms, and monotonicity is not needed.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J83 (Metric theory), 11J04. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a positive function f on the positive integers. A reduced approximation to α is p/q with q positive, gcd(p,q) = 1 and \|α−p/q\| &lt; f(q)/q. Its test series is ∑<sub>q≥1</sub> φ(q)f(q)/q, where φ(q) counts residues coprime to q.

**Problem.** For every f, almost every real α has infinitely many coprime solutions exactly when the totient series diverges. Khintchine’s test needs f to be monotone, since Duffin and Schaeffer found a non-monotone f whose series diverges while almost no α is approximable.

**How the definition helps.** Coprimality leaves φ(q) distinct reduced centers per unit interval at denominator q (our own). Their radii f(q)/q give the totient series. The Duffin–Schaeffer theorem of Koukoulopoulos and Maynard proves the divergence implication for arbitrary f.

It says: “Duffin and Schaeffer provided a famous counterexample to show that Khintchine's theorem fails without monotonicity assumption.”

### Unshifted pair correlations force uniformity

**Remember:** At zero shift the density pairs with itself.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K06 (General theory of distribution modulo \\(1\\)), 11K38. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix circle points x₁,x₂,… and a shift γ. Count ordered pairs of distinct indices i,j ≤ N with xᵢ−xⱼ within circular distance s/N of γ. Correlation is Poissonian at γ if this count divided by N tends to 2s for every s &gt; 0.

**Problem.** Poissonian pair correlation at zero forces uniform distribution. Each interval receives a limiting fraction of points equal to its length. For every nonzero shift modulo 1, some sequence has Poissonian pair correlation at that shift and fails uniform distribution.

**How the definition helps.** The shift parameter lets one statistic express both assertions (our own). The unshifted pair correlation theorem gives uniform distribution at zero. The cited shifted counterexample theorem supplies a nonuniform sequence for each nonzero shift.

**Paper or page:** [On Inhomogeneous Poissonian Pair Correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16542v1), [On Inhomogeneous Poissonian Pair Correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16542v1). It says: “that has γ-PPC but is not uniformly distributed.”

### Anchored variation gives exact quadrature error

**Remember:** A single box tests the sharpness of the integration bound.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On \[0,1)ᵈ, represent f as a constant plus a mixture of box indicators against a finite signed measure ν on (0,1\]ᵈ. The indicator at t tests whether x lies below t in every coordinate. Define variation as the infimum of the total unsigned mass of ν over all such representations.

**Problem.** The supremum of the absolute integration error over functions of variation at most one equals the star discrepancy. Integration error means sample average minus uniform integral. Star discrepancy is the supremum of the absolute frequency error over these boxes.

**How the definition helps.** The representation expresses integration error as an integral of box errors against ν (our own). Each box error is bounded in magnitude by star discrepancy, so taking the infimum gives the upper bound. A unit mass at each individual box recovers its error, giving the reverse bound upon taking the supremum.

**Wikipedia:** [Low-discrepancy sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-discrepancy_sequence). It says: “The Koksma–Hlawka inequality is sharp in the following sense”

### Dual digital nets retain exactly surviving frequencies

**Remember:** A Walsh frequency survives precisely when its induced input frequency is zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A binary digital net takes every u ∈ {0,1}ᵐ once and uses Cⱼu modulo two as coordinate j’s digits, followed by zeros. A Walsh mask k selects binary digits, giving value (−1) raised to their sum. The dual net consists of masks with ∑ⱼ Cⱼᵀkⱼ = 0 modulo two, using only digit positions present in each matrix.

**Problem.** The sample average of a Walsh function equals one for dual masks and zero otherwise. For an absolutely convergent series of Walsh functions, sample average minus uniform integral equals the sum of coefficients at nonzero dual masks.

**How the definition helps.** A dual mask gives even parity on every input (our own). Otherwise, flipping an input bit with nonzero coefficient pairs opposite signs. Absolute convergence permits termwise averaging, and only the constant Walsh function has nonzero uniform integral.

**Paper or page:** [Optimal periodic L²-discrepancy and diaphony bounds for higher order digital sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05747v1). It says: “and where 𝒟 is the so-called dual net”

### Extreme discrepancy removes lower-dimensional Haar terms

**Remember:** Taking differences of both box ends discards terms that ignore a coordinate.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F(t) be the sample fraction in \[0,t) minus its volume, where membership requires every coordinate to be below its threshold. Start with F and, one coordinate at a time, subtract the current function’s average in that coordinate. Call the result G.

**Problem.** For a box \[a,b), take its error as the sample fraction minus the volume. The integral of the squared error over all endpoint pairs with a ≤ b in every coordinate equals ∫\|G(t)\|² dt over the unit cube.

**How the definition helps.** Endpoint differences in all coordinates recover the box error and cancel every term removed by centering (our own). For mean-zero g, integrating \|g(b)−g(a)\|² over a ≤ b gives ∫\|g\|² by symmetry and expansion. Apply this identity in each coordinate to G, whose coordinate averages vanish.

**Paper or page:** [Point sets with optimal order of extreme and periodic discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.05781v1). It says: “and D its anchored discrepancy function with Haar coefficients”

**Sources:**

- [Point sets with optimal order of extreme and periodic discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.05781v1)

### Greedy squared error gives uniform distribution

**Remember:** Uniform averaging cancels the cross term before you choose the next point.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For each box \[0,t) in the unit cube, subtract N times its volume from its count among the first N points. Here \[0,t) contains points below t in every coordinate. Choose the next point to minimize the integral over t of the resulting squared error.

**Problem.** From any fixed nonempty finite starting list, the root mean square count error divided by N is O(N⁻¹⁄²). The fraction of points in each box approaches its volume.

**How the definition helps.** Squaring the error makes the cross term disappear when we average over a uniformly chosen next point (our own). At each box the random count increment minus its expected value has mean zero and absolute value at most one (our own). The minimum therefore increases the integrated squared error by at most one per step (our own). The cited theorem gives the resulting uniform distribution.

**Paper or page:** [Uniformly distributed sequences generated by a greedy minimization of the L² discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06298v4). It says: “is uniformly distributed modulo 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Uniformly distributed sequences generated by a greedy minimization of the L² discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06298v4)

### Index coordinates transfer discrepancy bounds

**Remember:** A box in the new coordinate selects a block of the old sequence.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Attach j/N to the jth point of a list indexed from zero. For any half-open box, subtract the expected count under uniform sampling from its actual count. Extreme L² discrepancy is the square root of the integral of this squared error over coordinatewise ordered endpoint pairs.

**Problem.** For every infinite sequence in the d-dimensional unit cube, infinitely many prefixes have extreme L² discrepancy at least c(d)(log N)ᵈ⁄². Here N is the prefix length and c(d) is positive.

**How the definition helps.** An interval in the added coordinate selects the difference of two prefixes (our own). Rounding its endpoints to indices changes the expected count by at most two (our own). The triangle inequality bounds the lifted discrepancy by twice the largest prefix discrepancy plus two (our own). The finite point theorem in dimension d+1 forces this maximum to grow at least as fast as (log N)ᵈ⁄² (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Exact order of extreme Lᵖ discrepancy of infinite sequences in arbitrary dimension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06461v1), [Point sets with optimal order of extreme and periodic discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.05781v1). It says: “for infinitely many N ∈ ℕ.”

**Sources:**

- [Exact order of extreme Lᵖ discrepancy of infinite sequences in arbitrary dimension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06461v1)

### Interlaced digits raise digital net order

**Remember:** Interlacing pushes the largest input digits up by nearly a factor α.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a binary digital net, a dual mask selects digit positions whose sum is even for every input. Its order-α weight sums the largest α selected positions per coordinate, using all positions when fewer occur. Interlacing groups α coordinates by moving position j in coordinate r to position α(j−1)+r, for 1 ≤ r ≤ α.

**Problem.** Suppose every nonzero dual mask of the original αd-dimensional net has order one weight greater than m−t′. Every nonzero dual mask of the interlaced d-dimensional net then has order α weight greater than αm−αt′−dα(α−1)/2.

**How the definition helps.** Splitting an output dual mask by these positions gives an input dual mask with the same parity test (our own). Each input coordinate’s leading position j moves to αj−(α−r). Each group’s largest α positions sum to at least the sum of those moved leaders. The loss per group is at most α(α−1)/2.

**Paper or page:** [Optimal periodic L²-discrepancy and diaphony bounds for higher order digital sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05747v1). It says: “is an order 1 digital (t′, αd)-sequence over ℤ₂”

**Sources:**

- [Optimal periodic L²-discrepancy and diaphony bounds for higher order digital sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05747v1)

### Low discrepancy forces mesoscopic counts

**Remember:** At a wider scale, each point sees the expected number of neighbors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix 0 &lt; β &lt; 1 and s &gt; 0. Among the first N points of a circle sequence, count ordered pairs of distinct indices at circular distance at most s/Nᵝ. Divide by N raised to 2 − β.

**Problem.** Suppose the largest absolute difference between sample fraction and length over all arcs is o(N⁻ᵝ). Then the normalized count tends to 2s for every fixed s &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** The chosen radius makes each test arc longer than the discrepancy error, uniformly over its center (our own). Each center therefore sees 2sN¹⁻ᵝ + o(N¹⁻ᵝ) points including itself (our own). Summing over centers counts ordered pairs, and removing the N self-pairs does not affect the limit (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Weak Poissonian box correlations of higher order](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.11105v2). It says: “Then the sequence has (k, β)-Poissonian box correlations”

### Normalized height lets roots reflect

**Remember:** Reflect through the unit circle without changing angles or normalized height.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a monic polynomial P with P(0) ≠ 0, use the height h(P) = ∫₀¹ log⁺(\|P(exp(2πit))\|/√\|P(0)\|) dt. Here log⁺ means the positive part of the logarithm.

**Problem.** Replace each root r outside the unit disk by 1/r̄ and take the monic polynomial with the resulting roots. This preserves height and every angular sector count. Thus the degree-N angular count bound 4√(Nh(P)/π) reduces to the case of roots in the closed unit disk.

**How the definition helps.** For \|z\| = 1, reflection preserves \|z−r\|/√\|r\| and the argument of r (our own). Multiplying these factors preserves the normalized boundary modulus and hence its height. Reflection also preserves every angular count with multiplicity, so the estimate inside the disk applies.

**Paper or page:** [Hilbert transforms and the equidistribution of zeros of polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00105v4). It says: “If P is a monic polynomial of degree N with P(0) ≠ 0, then 𝒟(P) ≤ (4/√π)√(N h(P)).”

### Pure eigenvalues bound hyper-Kloosterman sums

**Remember:** The sum is a signed trace of r eigenvalues of the same size.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a prime p, an integer r ≥ 3 and a ∈ 𝔽ₚˣ. The hyper-Kloosterman sum Kᵣ(a) sums exp(2πi(x₁+⋯+xᵣ)/p) over all tuples in (𝔽ₚˣ)ʳ with product a. A Frobenius action is pure of weight w if every eigenvalue has complex absolute value p raised to w/2.

**Problem.** The absolute value of Kᵣ(a) is at most r times p to the power (r−1)/2.

**How the definition helps.** The trace formula expresses the sum through eigenvalues, so their number and sizes give a bound. Deligne’s theorem supplies the difficult facts about this vector space, called cohomology with compact support. Only degree r−1 contributes, its dimension is r, and every eigenvalue has absolute value p to the power (r−1)/2. In our own final step, the signed trace satisfies the triangle inequality.

**Paper or page:** [The sixth moment of Dirichlet L-functions at the central point](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.01457v1). It says: “where the hyper-Kloosterman sum”

### Rank and purity bound Kloosterman sums

**Remember:** Rank counts the eigenvalues and purity bounds their sizes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations), 11T23, 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite field 𝔽𝓆 and nontrivial additive character ψ, the rank-r Kloosterman sum at a ∈ 𝔽𝓆ˣ sums ψ(x₁+⋯+xᵣ) over tuples with product a. Purity of weight w means every Frobenius eigenvalue at a rational point has complex modulus q raised to w/2.

**Problem.** For r ≥ 2 the sum has modulus at most r times q raised to (r − 1)/2.

**How the definition helps.** The sheaf expresses every sum as a signed trace, so its rank and the sizes of its eigenvalues give one uniform bound. Our own deduction uses Deligne’s theorem that the sheaf has rank r and every Frobenius eigenvalue has modulus q raised to (r − 1)/2. The triangle inequality finishes the estimate.

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “Geometrically the sum is taken along a 'hyperbola' XY = ab”

**Remember:** Chebyshev polynomials remove the invariant part of ordinary moments.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations), 11T23, 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For odd prime p, nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽ₚ and a ∈ 𝔽ₚˣ, put K(a) = ∑ₓ ψ(x+a/x) over x ∈ 𝔽ₚˣ. Define θ(a) ∈ \[0,π\] by 2cos θ(a) = −K(a)/√p. Define Uₘ(cos θ) = sin((m+1)θ)/sin θ by continuity at both endpoints.

**How the definition helps.** The polynomial Uₘ turns each angle into the trace on degree-m symmetric tensors, which have no invariant vector for the determinant-one group SL(2). Our own calculation adds the eigenvalues exp(i(m − 2j)θ) for 0 ≤ j ≤ m. Katz identifies the geometric symmetry group of the normalized Kloosterman system as SL(2). The trace formula and Deligne’s bound then give the stated cancellation.

### Zeta roots bound Kloosterman sums

**Remember:** The first coefficient is the negative sum of the two reciprocal roots.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a prime p and a,b ∈ 𝔽ₚˣ. For every r ≥ 1, let S(r) sum exp(2πiTr(ax+b/x)/p) over x ∈ 𝔽ₚʳˣ, using the trace to 𝔽ₚ. The associated L-function is the formal series L(t) = exp(∑<sub>r≥1</sub> S(r)tʳ/r).

**Problem.** There are complex numbers α and β of absolute value √p such that L(t) = (1−αt)(1−βt). Consequently \|S(1)\| ≤ 2√p.

**How the definition helps.** The generating series puts the original sum in its linear coefficient. Weil’s work on the curve yᵖ−y = ax+b/x gives the factorization and the sizes of α and β. In our own coefficient comparison, S(1) = −α−β. The triangle inequality gives the estimate.

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “A fundamental technique of Weil reduces the estimate \|K(a,b;p)\| ≤ 2√p, when ab ≠ 0 to his results on local zeta-functions.”

**Remember:** A prime cube can support a sum larger than the square-root bound.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a fixed k ≥ 3, call q cube-free if no prime cube divides it. Let f be an integer polynomial of degree at most k whose nonconstant coefficients have no common factor with q.

**Problem.** For cube-free q, the complete sum of exp(2πif(x)/q) over x modulo q is O(q to the power ½+ε) for every ε &gt; 0. The constant depends on k and ε. At q = p³ with prime p &gt; 3, the phase x³ instead gives the sum p².

**How the definition helps.** Cube-freeness leaves only primes and prime squares in the standard complete-sum estimate (our own). Modulo p³, group the cubic phase by residue classes modulo p². Each class of units cancels by additive character orthogonality, while each of the p² multiples of p contributes one.

### One critical moment controls all

**Remember:** Below the critical moment use Hölder, and above it use the maximum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For positive integers k,N and α ∈ \[0,1\]ᵏ, put F(α) = ∑<sub>n=1</sub>ᴺ exp(2πi∑<sub>j=1</sub>ᵏ αⱼnʲ). Its moment M(p) is the integral of \|F(α)\|ᵖ over the unit cube. The critical order is 2K with K = k(k+1)/2.

**Problem.** Suppose M(2K) ≤ Cε Nᴷ⁺ᵋ for every ε &gt; 0. Then M(2s) ≤ C Nᵐ⁺ᵋ for every fixed s &gt; 0 and ε &gt; 0, where m = max(s,2s−K). Constants may depend on k, ε and the chosen order.

**How the definition helps.** At the critical order the two predicted powers of N coincide, so one estimate covers both ranges. In our own reduction, Hölder’s inequality on a cube of volume one bounds M(2s) by M(2K) to the power s/K below that order. Above it, bound the extra factors using \|F\| ≤ N. The deep mean-value theorem supplies the critical estimate.

**Paper or page:** [Decoupling estimates in Fourier analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00652v1). It says: “N<sup>1/2</sup> + N<sup>{1</sup> - \\frac{k(k+1)}{2p}}”

### Reduced phases exclude constant counterexamples

**Remember:** Over the prime field, remove powers of p before using the degree.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over the field with p elements, replace each monomial degree that is positive and divisible by p by that degree divided by p. Repeat until no such degree remains and combine equal powers. Call the resulting polynomial reduced and exclude constant reduced polynomials.

**Problem.** If the reduced phase has degree d ≥ 1, the complete sum of exp(2πif(x)/p) has absolute value at most (d−1)√p. A nonconstant original phase need not qualify, since xᵖ−x gives sum p.

**How the definition helps.** Over 𝔽ₚ, xᵖ = x preserves each monomial’s values under reduction (our own). Thus xᵖ−x reduces to zero and the nonconstant-degree requirement excludes it. Every surviving leading degree is coprime to p, so Weil’s estimate applies.

**Wikipedia:** [Fermat's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_little_theorem). It says: “aᵖ ≡ a (mod p).”
